reviewText: My 3-yr-old daughter was extremely excited to see this toy come out of the box. She loves Mickey and Minnie, and was just so excited to play with the clubhouse. THE Clubhouse, in fact. She did play with this toy for about a half an hour by herself. After that, she played with it along with her grandparents (who had some trouble understanding how it worked).Assembly was fairly simple: attach the slide, put the microphone on the stand, and attach the airplane to the big Mickey head. The directions were printed on the side of the box -- a great idea for getting rid of paper directions, but it took me a minute to find them.It took me a minute to understand how the slide works. The figures go inside the red hatch at the top, and when you push down on the purple stand on the side of the Mickey head, the Toodles hatch opens up for the character to come out and down the slide.So -- a cute toy, overall. But, it's not really a great toy, and certainly not what I've come to expect from Fischer Price.Here are the issues we've encountered:The Plane: A neat idea, having a plane that you can put a character into that goes around the head. The first problem was that my daughter didn't understand how to get a character into the plane. Their legs do bend, and then you can sit them in the plane (sort of). They don't fit well in the seat because their hips are too wide (Mickey and Minnie both). As a result, the characters fall out of the plane on the downswing around the head. The other issue is that my kids were able to get the plane detached from the head. This would not be great for a 2-yr-old who might want to stick the plane attachment in their mouth.The Slide: Characters do not actually slide down the slide after coming out of the hatch. They fall out onto the stop of the slide, where they stay until the kids push them down the slide. The 3-yr-old wasn't too perturbed by this, but I certainly was.The Hatch: It's not easy to get the characters into the top of the hatch because their arms stick out a little wide for that. You can work them in, but it's not an easy fit. The grandparents were not sure how to open the hatch -- they figured it out eventually, but then they didn't realize that it could be closed up again.The Head: Grandparents complained that the toy tipped over easily. The door opening on the side is cute and allows for lots of pretend play with characters showing up to the clubhouse for a visit. There is a handle on the top of the head, which is nice for the person that cleans up the toys (namely, mom), but it's not like the toy is self-contained. It comes with a teeter-totter (see-saw) and a table and chairs for the characters to sit in, but it's not like you can store them inside the head and take them around without them falling out.The majority of the problems with the toy can be traced back to the characters: they're too big and too heavy. We plan on using other characters from other toys when we play with this toy. The kids are not too upset by the problems we encountered, they just play like they always do. Even so, I don't know how much replay this toy is going to get once the novelty factor wears off.

reviewText: My daughter has always enjoyed Fisher-Price Little People brand items.  The little characters, and the various toys always seem to draw her in.  We like them because they are usually well thought out and usually quite durable.Now on to this specific one.  Disney has combined with Fisher-Price to create the Disney Princess theme.  A lot of you may be opposed to the 'princessification' of our children, but this set is mostly harmless.  It comes in a small box, lots of pieces, including multiple steps, multiple screws and so on to put together.  Shouldn't take more than 10-15 minutes, but annoying nevertheless.  Then there is the sticker sheet, where you have to go put the stickers it should have came with from the factory on the the toy.  I always mess these up.It comes with the Castle, a couple of chairs (thrones?) a bed (with great inserts that the princesses fit into perfectly).  It also comes with Snow White and Cindarella Little People figurines.  The castle itself has multiple sounds (also high/low for sound volume..both of which are quite loud), when you open the doors, when the tea kettle is pushed, and then when you put two princesses on and make them dance.  There is also the piece that you can put the princesses on and it will tell you their name, and if you keep pushing it, some more information or a song about them.  You can buy additional princesses for this as well, I believe there are ~10 total.Some annoying things.  The flags don't like to stay affixed to the top of the castle, the furniture doesn't really seem to fit and will probably be easily lost.  The 'elevator' is kind of cheap, and it my 2 1/2 year old daughter can't easily operate it, but she doesn't care much about it either.Overall it gets a lot of play time, doesn't take up all that much space.  If you're looking for both a boy and girl, the Zoo Talkers Little People series is probably a better fit, but the girls will love this one.

reviewText: I still remember Yahtzee games from forty years ago and the excited yell of anyone who rolled the coveted "Yahtzee" - five dice with the same number.Twenty years ago I bought aYahtzeegame for my own family - and it was just like I remembered it.  Which would have been fine for circa 1970, but in the video game era is frankly a little slow.  You wait YOUR turn while all the other players in the game take their three (or less) rolls of the dice.  There is a bit of strategy to it, but the degree to which blind luck determines a game was hammered home to me recently when I downloaded an electronic version of the game for a handheld device - not as fun as the game I remembered from my childhood.This new Yahtzee game adds action and excitement to the relatively stale concept: all players roll at once and an electronic button in the center of the playing board allows players to jump in and claim needed dice combinations.  This game keeps the best parts of old Yahtzee and adds needed excitement.  Good for old Yahtzee fans and anyone looking for an exciting dice game.

There is a bit of strategy to it, but the degree to which blind luck determines a game was hammered home to me recently when I downloaded an electronic version of the game for a handheld device - not as fun as the game I remembered from my childhood.This new Yahtzee game adds action and excitement to the relatively stale concept: all players roll at once and an electronic button in the center of the playing board allows players to jump in and claim needed dice combinations. This game keeps the best parts of old Yahtzee and adds needed excitement. Good for old Yahtzee fans and anyone looking for an exciting dice game.

reviewText: Several years back, I bought the original Spot It for my niece. It turned out to be so much fun that even the adults got into the action. So when I saw this Junior edition, my interest was piqued. Especially since my daughter is 4-years-old.The two decks are very similar. The biggest difference is that Spot It Junior uses animals, so it's easier for younger kids to identify. There are also 24 fewer cards (31 vs. 55), making the game go by quicker (a reason why Junior is slightly less expensive). Because of this, the max amount of players is six instead of eight.There are five ways to play this game, three of them for children ages four and older, and two for children ages six and older (since they are a little more advanced).My daughter absolutely loves this game, and it's enjoyable for my wife and I when we play it with her. If you are buying this for a child over six years of age, I recommend getting the regular Spot It game instead.
summary: A great game for children! (and the adults who play it with them)

reviewText: The LeapFrog LeapReader Writing Workbook teaches numbers and some basic reading and math skills.  It requires using theLeapFrog LeapReader Reading and Writing System, which is an electronic pen with audio.  It is indeed part of a system, and requires online registration, but is a different system from the LeapFrog TAG reading system, even though it looks somewhat similar.  If you are buying this as a gift, talk to the parent first, to make sure it is compatible.  There are over 150 different activity books available for the system.This book is fun to use, but the children will require some adult assistance.  The educational value is very good, with an emphasis on actually writing numbers.  Remember how hard it was to make a good-looking "8" or "5"?  This provides a template and immediate feedback based on the actual strokes.  A couple of dozen practice pages are included.

reviewText: Both my 3 year old nephew and my 6 year old niece enjoy playing with this toy.  The remote control is in the shape of a stop/go sign that the child holds up or down to control the truck.  The fireman in the truck spins around when it is in motion, so to make it go in another direction you have to stop and start it.  There was a bit of a learning curve until they both figured that out but now they've got it down pat.They've been using it on hardwood floors and have had no problem using it on that surface.  It's taken a header down a flight of six stairs onto a tile floor and didn't seem the worse for wear; it's also rammed into furniture often and I haven't seen any damage to it (or to the furniture). I've seen it in use often when the firetruck fleet comes out to play.  I've also seen them using the stop/go sign when they play other games; my nephew was holding it up when my niece and I were throwing a ball to one another and he wanted to cross in front of us when he was using his toy lawnmower (he specifically went and got the sign to use for that purpose).Both kids usually wind up laughing as they watching the firetruck dart around in various directions, usually chasing one or another of them (or me - lol).

I haven't tried it yet, so I can't say for sure if it works.2) The other thing is if you leave the stickers stuck on the scene pages (and don't put them back on the white pages they originally come on)they leave an oily looking gray stain on the picture scenes.3) In addition, the binding is cheap.  Neither set we own are no longer in book form; I just have a bunch of loose pages.  Which isn't a huge deal, but is a little annoying once the stickers start loosing their stickiness and you can no longer keep them contained by turning the whole pad upside down (when still sealed, the binding kept the loose stickers in like a manila filing folder).I mention those things because I could see how those big things could bother some kids or some parents.  Overall, I still think it is a good value and I would buy it again.

reviewText: My toddler really never grew to be that interested with the alligator (other than trying to scare Mommy with him - ha) - at least not as a walking toy.  He does make a cool clacking sound when you pull him - but I don't know...not sure why he seems so popular.  We did have fun taking our Learning Resources Gingerbread snap toys and placing them in each of the openings on the alligator's back - and that's really all my 2 year old uses him for.  We've had him for a year and I've tried to get her engaged in pulling him around.  The colors are bright and he seems very sturdy... I just don't think the toy is worth the price.  That said, I only have one child (so far) - so maybe it's just a matter of my baby not being into pull toys.  She much preferred walking around using a helium balloon to have the similar effect as a pull toy - so go figure! :)

reviewText: My 1 year old daughter has not stopped playing with this cafe since she received it 6 days ago. She dances every time that Elmo, Abbie and Cookie Monster sing the catchy (but not annoying) songs. My four year old son also plays with her and this keeps them both entertained for long periods of time. This toy is designed for younger children and because of the smaller size, would be a great choice for a first kitchen. This cafe comes with a toy frying pan, spatula, a salmon filet, a slice of veggie pizza, a cheese & tomato slice, a fried egg and an oatmeal cookie. The monsters request to be fed certain snacks and the kids are able to "feed" them by  putting the toy food in their mouths and then it slides down into the oven. This toy is cute, fun and has great sound effects such as a sizzling stove top and a bell ring indicating the order is up. This is a huge hit in our household!

reviewText: I ordered this for my 3 year old, thinking that he would probably like it but that it would soon end up in a big pile with his other toys.  I was wrong.  I'm not sure what it is about the weebles that is so appealing, but when I got home yesterday, all three of my kids (3, 5, and 6) were gathered around the play house, all playing (more or less) contentedly with it.  Weebles were wobbling but not falling, the crank was fun for them all to try to put not only weebles but also some of their toy cars in, and the slide was a playground for weebles and army men alike.  THe bright colors were attractive, and fortunately for my three boys, the whole thing is quite sturdy.  We are usually quite hard on toys, but this hasn't broken in a week of hard play by three rambunctious boys, which is more than I can say for a lot of other kids toys that are supposed to be sturdy.  I have to say, I'm very pleased with this toy, and I'm glad we got it.  I recommend it to anyone with kids 4 and under (although my 6 year old likes it, I think he mostly just likes having something acceptable to play with his two brothers), and best of all--no sound effects.
summary: Surprisingly broad appeal and lasting fun from a simple product!

reviewText: First of all, I would like to say that I enjoy a good game of UNO, but could not get into this version as it was designed.  Other reviewers have said that they have really enjoyed it (4.5+ stars overall), but for me, it was too confining in its ability to let a game "happen".  You have to start by recording your names into the robot - come up with house rules (or use the ones on the cards) - a "Max" volume level that does not even allow you to play a game at a party or with large gathering of people due to the low output of the speaker - etc...  With regular UNO there are no names to be recorded and completely random gameplay if you choose to do so.  I gave this Robot version only 3 of 5 stars, because if you find a quiet enough setting to play it in, then it could be a good time.  The 3 stars were given due to the ability to be able to play UNO with or without the robot (ie: only the cards).  UNO is a game that can stand on its own or be played in variety of ways that does not include a gimick.
summary: Not the best version of UNO

reviewText: This is a fun game, it is like a combination of Ticket to Ride, Monopoly, and Settlers of Catan.You have to use your money to build power plants and connect cities.  You also have to bid on power plants.  Power plants use resources coal, oil, trash, and uranium or renewable resource.  You have to buy resources to power your cities.  In return you get money for the number of cities you supply.This game has very unique gameplay.  It is very replayable, resources replenish depending on the number of players.  The resources get consumed based on what other players buy, but like in real life the prices are based on demand.  if multiple players are using coal, coal can get very expensive, but if no one is using oil it could get very cheap.This is not a good intro game into gaming of this type, I think this game would be easier to pick up if you are familiar with Ticket to Ride and Settlers of Catan.  But this is a must have game if you are into board games.

reviewText: I got this unit to replace one that wasn't nearly as much fun, not being sure if my 26 month old grandson would be quite ready for it.No problem there! He is so thrilled with it. The colors are bright and vivid right out of the markers and when the light feature is turned on he says tada and his face is the only thing brighter than the art screen.The gel markers wipe off skin and oopsies on the table top do too.The only problem he has is getting the caps off the markers as the caps are kind of small - but I'm always there to help anyway.The light board has a number of flashing sequences and a steady light also - lots of fun after dark and would be a great car trip, camping activity, but the light is bright enough to make an impact in the daylight too.There is an easel feature but that's kind of wobbly to draw on but works as a display stand and also has the ability to be hung on a wall if you wanted to do that.If I was to change one thing it would be the size of the markers. I think making them fatter and the caps larger would make it easier for a little guys hand size although I would definitely keep the fine tips as they are excellent for making lines.When the board is ready to be erased, the easiest way I found is to use a damp wash cloth first and then wife with a paper towel. It only takes a minute to clean up and that's good because that's about all the time he gives me before starting his next work of art.

reviewText: This is the cutest toy "piano" yet!  When you push the keys a little ball pops up in a tube on the top.  The keys are all different colors and each have a different number on them (1-8). The balls are the same color as the corresponding key. You can set the toy to Low or High according to your preference and leave it on. The sound stops after a minute of inactivity but can be reactivated by pressing any button on the keyboard. There are 4 different modes:  Numbers/Counting, Music, Creativity and Colors.  This is a great way to learn numbers and colors and also to learn some fun preschool songs.  Our littlest one loves this.  She doesn't have enough language to learn the songs or colors or numbers yet but she loves the "action" and the sounds.  Our older preschooler is able to repeat the learning elements and purely loves the songs.  This is a great toy for learning and just plain enjoyment!.

reviewText: UPDATE 5/16/2011My review of Fridge Words haven't changed, as it's still working great.  My problem, however, is if you ever lose a letter.  We recently lost the "f", and Leapfrog won't replace it.  According to their website, they can't replace the letter and there's pretty much nothing I can do about it.  This is not a huge problem, however my kids did notice the letter missing...*sigh*.  So, spelling words like "fox", "fun", and "far" is temporarily hindered.  I'm not about to go buying a new set, and have scoured eBay for the replacement - most resellers sell individual letter for about $2 each, not including shipping.  That said - watch out for those lost letters!!!!-------------------------------We purchased the Leapfrog Fridge Words Magnetic Word Builder in 2008 for our son for Christmas.  It's now 2010, the toy is still working great, and now our 1 1/2 year old daughter is playing with it, too!  There are a lot of appealing features about this toy for our kids; the little music notes button sings the full ABC song, the letters are easy to put into the slots, and music and voices on the toy are fun for the kids to listen to.  Our daughter likes to push the music button and sing and dance along with the song.  Our son who is now almost 3 is just starting to understand to put the correct letter into the slot when playing the spelling mode.  There are three modes to this toy - listening to letter when putting it into any slot, spelling any three letter word, and spelling a three letter word that is specified.We do have a few gripes about this toy, particularly with the sound quality of the toy.  Some words are just flat out hard to understand.  I've had to listen to some of the words twice to decipher whether the word given was lap or pat or whatever.  I can only imagine how hard it is for our kids to decipher!  It would also be nice to have the modes switch placed somewhere else on the toy.  Our kids like to switch up modes - usually to a harder mode that they can't figure out yet - and treats the switch as a plaything!  While this is nice to encourage play, I would rather have our kids focus on playing and learning the letters/phonetics instead of switching to a mode where they hear "beep beep!  whoops, let's try another one!" all the time.Outside of those gripes, the toy is well made, educational, and our kids like playing with it.  Recommended!
summary: Some words hard to understand, but overall good toy

reviewText: When I first saw my kids playing the Solve It With Elmo game, I wasn't sure they'd like it.  The initial game of choosing an object of the right weight to launch Super Grover into the air seemed too plain to hold their interest.  But I was wrong.  They enjoy launching Super Grover from his lever and then catching toys with the net.  The game then moves on to other stages where the children solve simple puzzles and are introduced to different types of physics tools like the wheel and the pulley.The game is definitely better suited for 4-7 year old children, but it holds their interest fairly well. My 3 year old plays it, though she doesn't fully understand it.  My 5 year old enjoys it, and my 7 year old plays it even though I thought it might be too repetitive for her.  As they proceed through the game, they earn more badges and micro-mods.This game introduces children (including my 9 and 11 year old sons) to the science of physics.  My initial assessment of it being too repetitive was wrong, though I think older kids will be turned off by the characters more than the game itself.
summary: Physics made fun and simple for kids.

reviewText: The Complete Kids Campfire is one of a number of products designed to allow children to pretend they're camping - even when inside. Other items from the product manufacturer  include indoor tents, lanterns, and more.I've always loved toys like these ( toy drills or ovens are other examples) which are springboards for kids' imagination. Television and video games have their place, too, but children who have a chance to enact their own adventures...including camping...are lucky indeed.With the Complete Kids Campfire, aspiring campers can gather their "supplies" and go camping inside - even on the coldest, snowiest days. It can sometimes be a challenge to find unique toys that appeal to kids. The campfire kit fills that gap. It does, however,have one feature I'd like changed -a motor noise from a built- in fan. And that noise could be a deal breaker.For potential buyers who might worry that even a safe, artificial (but very realistic looking) campfire could encourage children to play with fire, I'd argue the opposite. Instead, this toy provides the perfect opportunity to discuss fire safety. The enclosed product literature even has link to a U.S. Fire Administration (USFA) website page focused on educating both parents and children about basic fire safety. Impressive!. The website is also noted on the package itself.As for the toy campfire, here's a quick rundown of the major features:Pros:1. Realistic "flame" created by a wispy, flame-shaped fabric which moves just like the flickering orange glow of a fire (with the help of a battery-powered fan concealed in the toy).2. The campfire is packaged in a box with an orange background, perfect for using as back drop to make the "fire" look very awesome and even more spectacular.3. Even kids living in city apartments or homes far from the country can pretend they're camping. Now all kids, city or country dwellers, can play at camping...no matter what the weather.4. Ready to use  right out of the package, complete with batteries. Nothing extra to buy.5. As noted before, an excellent toy for pretend play, offering a great option to television and a way to relieve boredom when bad weather prevents outside play....if the noise factor can be ignored..the motor sound.7. Can be used by more than one child at a time or with parents who want to get in on the fun.Cons:I have only one suggestion to take this product from fun to phenomenal...get rid of the noisy motor sound and substitute something that simulates a crackling fire.
summary: Realistic looking fire but too noisy and not in a good, fun way

reviewText: My 2 1/2 year old twins LOVE Mickey Mouse Clubhouse, so I was very happy to have the opportunity to review this clubhouse.  First, the clubhouse does look just like it does on TV, so kids who watch the show will immediately know what it is.  The colors are bright and kid pleasing, and the assembly is not difficult.  The plastic that the clubhouse is made of is not "heavy duty" so the whole clubhouse seems a bit flimsy, but it has held up nicely to spirited play by 2 1/2 year old twins.My complaints with the toy is the same as other reviewers, the figures will not stay in the plane unless you tightly wedge them in the airplane, and my toddlers can not manage this on their own.  There has also been difficulty getting the figures to slide down the slide.  All in all, these issues have not seemed to decrease my toddler's enjoyment of this toy.  We have several "Farmer" Mickey, Donald, and Goofy toys, and the figures from those also work with this playset.  All in all, we are happy with this toy.

reviewText: I missed the original Bop It when I was a child...I ordered this as a whim for my kids and stuck it in a closet and forgot about it.  My daughter's friend said she wanted one for Xmas and I was like, "We have one."  Little did I know my daughter had been playing one at a friend's house!  We packed it for a trip and when I brought it out, everyone wanted to play.  My cousins were like, Bop It, this was so much fun when we were kids!  My kids are 8 and 6- they love it along with my cousins who are in their early 20s.  I can't imagine the standard version being much fun (it one has three different things to do) but this one is definitely challenging.  My only critical comment is that the "shake it" option does not seem as responsive as the others.  Definitely would recommend.  The adults watching loved hearing the random comments made by the Bop It.

reviewText: I have two children who are passionate about science so we have had and have many, many, many, many science kits. This is not on our top 20 list of favorites. There are less expensive sets that have been more fun, educational, and required less planning than this one.The strong points of this set are the gimmicky mixing containers, such as the toilet and trash can, and the very well done full color instruction booklet.The weak points are that while the ingredients are common household items, they are not common household items we always have in our cabinets. Some of the items we do not keep on hand were:purple cabbagecarbonated waterdisposable diaperdry yeastunflavored gelatininstant coffeenavy beansnonfat evaporated milkMost of the experiments worked as described when we followed the directions. Some did not work. Some worked in a very unimpressive way (I'm talking to you, "Whirling Technicolor Moo Juice").Many of these experiments are widely available on the internet, Youtube, or Pinterest. The molds and mixers are gimmicky in a way that even turned off my 8 year old.If you are looking for a rainy day set to hold your kids' attention for about 10 minutes, this does have quite the listing of experiments. You could always supplement the book with online videos if you are trying to make it more educational. Overall, I would not recommend this set to a friend.

reviewText: This is a great group/family/classroom game for ages 5 and up. The game is called "Don't Make Me Laugh" but the actual point of the game is the laugh, be creative, and have fun.The basic game procedure is to work alone or in pairs or small groups, then one at a time draw from three card piles (Solo, Partner, All) and act out whatever is on the card. Here are some examples of Solo Play: Pretend you are walking in high heels for the first time (especially good for younger children and boys/men) or pretend you are a race car driver and you win the race. An example from Partner Play: Pretend to be a waiter and customer and the customer is ordering mud pie, or pretend you are both kernels of pop corn and you are popping in slow motion. An example from ALL Play: Pretend you are dancing in the rain, or pretend you just ate really hot chili peppers.At the end of each round, players can choose and award tokens to other players for best performance, most enthusiastic performance, silliest performance, bravest performance, and most creative performance.  There are colored, cloth "baskets" to hold tokens, and there are colored plastic bands for participants to wear to show what group they are in (3 per color). There is also a plastic clown nose to heighten the fun. At the end of all playing, the person with the most tokens "wins".Positives: Excellent for families, groups, and classrooms. Encourages everyone to participate - even shy or really young folks can work with a partner. Encourages creativity, vocabulary development, logical and diverse thinking, and imagination/role play.Negative: The game instructions encourage a winner, which means there are losers. Instead of giving the tokens, I don't use these and just verbally encourage discussion and who did what at the end of play. I don't use the tokens or award cards at all. Also the clown nose is made of a rigid plastic instead of a soft plastic so it hurts to wear. This clown nose is an expensive and completely unnecessary part of the game. Besides, if multiple people wear it, you are distributing germs and illness. The wrist bands are a waste of money and materials. It shows that the developers are talking down to the users in that people won't know what team they are on without a wristband. Even a 5 year old knows his or her team. And this is marketed as a "family" game, so the bands are a waste of time from this point of view. However, in a classroom setting, one band could be given to each "leader" of a group.So I don't use the nose, or bands, or tokens, or token containers. So literally half of the game is wasted money and materials from a purely family point of view.However, if you are a teacher or group facilitator and you are working with a group of 10 or more - say a class of 30 students - then all of the extra materials could come in handy. As a retired teacher, I see that this game would be great in after-school activities, drama classes, in-class for discussion and role/play because this is not a gender specific game so boys have to pretend to wear high heels and girls have to pretend to drive race cars or build houses etc. With that said, the marketing should reflect that this is a family and classroom game.I would still avoid using the clown nose….

reviewText: My daughter received this toy for her 2nd birthday 5 months ago and she has been playing with it constantly ever since. She throws birthday parties for mommy or daddy or the dog. She decorates and serves everyone slices and has the birthday girl (or boy, or dog) blow out the candles. Her 4 year old cousin has also played with and enjoyed this toy and I think it would be appropriate for children up to age 7. It is sturdy, easy for little hands to play with and easy to decorate with stick on jelly beans, gumdrops, strawberries and candles. Aside from being a magnet for dog hair we have had no problems with the velcro, and while the server isn't really functional for picking up slices, my daughter will happily pick up a slice of cake and put it on the server before she passes it on. She probably plays with this toy more than any other birthday present and I would definitely recommend it to other parents looking for a well made toy that encourages creative play.

I'm sure the limited possibilities will eventually bore my kids, but they haven't yet.

reviewText: Bottom line: I took a 100 piece Ravensburger puzzle and worked on it with this mat and it worked for me.  I would recommend.  There are a couple secrets to its success, and one limiting factor.This is really a simple product - almost too simple.  It consists of a HUGE blue felt mat, an inflatable center piece, and three elastic straps.  All you do is lay out the blue felt and keep the puzzle pieces 7 inches away from the edge.  (To give a sense of scale, I was able to barely place every one of the 1000 Ravensburger puzzle pieces on the blue mat, but couldn't adhere to the 7 inch rule.)  When you're ready to put the puzzle away, you place the inflatable center along the inside edge, and roll tightly and slowly.  Because of the length of the mat, watch out for slack developing on either end.  Once rolled up, secure with the three elastic bands.  This is best done by two people in order to maintain tension on the rolled puzzle.  I don't think a lot of pressure is needed, and compressing things could damage your pieces.  I just removed slack and kept things finger tight.In my test, I had mostly un-assembled pieces rolled up (figuring assembled will not be enough challenge in my test).  Once rolled up, I tried to get puzzle pieces to fall out.  I did get one to slip out, but this is after tossing it in the air, rotating the roll, and shaking it, far beyond the due care you should use when you have hundreds of puzzle pieces rolled in a thin mat!  Upon unrolling, my small built pieces were fine - just curved a bit, but no apparent damage.  The diameter of the inflatable piece seems to work with the puzzle pieces to minimize impact.  All my other pieces were still in the correct orientation so they likely didn't move much.  The felt has enough friction to keep things still.The only (small) downside is the size of the roll.  The trick they use here is to use a giant mat so to keep pieces away from the edge and thus from falling out, so the large size is the obvious downside.  But you can store your puzzle out of reach.  And when done, the mat folds up and the inflatable cigar piece easily deflates and stores in the provided puzzle-style box.  This will nicely sit on your puzzle shelf in good company for the next use.

reviewText: I picked this up for my three year-old Son, who is fanatical about Super-Heroes in general, and Spider-Man in particular. First off, it's not a very good idea to get this if you have a younger child that still puts things in his or her mouth, because these toys are a definite choking hazard. There's really not much here...you basically bounce the character pieces around trying to knock things over. My Son got bored with it and walked away after 5 minutes.......This is probably one of the most bizarre toy concepts I've ever seen. I would have loved to be there when the idea was pitched to the toy company. That must have been a hilarious meeting. There's not much here for kids of any age to enjoy.

I was positive I was looking for a whimsy with the shape of a dog's head with floppy ears, and it turned out to be the rear end of a giraffe (I know, that's hard to believe, and yet it's true).  Or, there were some whimsies with straight edges (including a square!) which were tricky to piece together without having the whole area done and fooled me occasionally into thinking they were border pieces.  So sometimes the whimsies seem to make things easier, but at least as often they are tricky.As far as the puzzle goes, it's about average in difficulty for the piece-count with large swaths all about the same color, but the pieces do snap together satisfyingly and the cutting of the pieces was smooth and clear.  None of the pieces were still stuck together when I opened the box.  We enjoyed putting this one together.

reviewText: I had been looking at purchasing this for quite some time and when I saw it on sale before Christmas 2012 I decided to go for it.  It was a great decision.  I had been looking to find a case for my old iPhone that I was no longer using so that my daughter could use it (2 years old) without having to worry about her dropping it or turning it off.  I love the fact that you can put the phone in two ways (one that has the home button accessible and one that doesn't).  I also like that it is relatively easy for an adult to remove the phone from the case for charging etc, but difficult for a child to do.  This is used on a daily basis in my home.  Fisher Price has some really good iPhone apps, which my daughter loves.  This is a great supplement to learning her ABCs, numbers, colors, shapes in a fun way. My only, very small complaints, are that you have to take the phone out to charge it or change the volume.  This can become annoying when she switches apps and the volume is different.  Overall, highly recommended.

reviewText: Hasbro's Playskool Weebles Musical Treehouse Playset is recommended for children 18 months and up. My granddaughter is 27 months old and she loves it. It was easy to unbox and assemble and assembly literally took less than 2 minutes (I knew beforehand from looking at Hasbro's product page to have 3 AA batteries ready as they are required but not included, and because I always keep my Leatherman multi-tool handy I had a Phillips head screwdriver - also required for assembly - ready to go). My granddaughter took to the Playset immediately (something that I can't say about all the toys I've given her and that she otherwise gets), letting out a delighted sounding "Wheeeee!" every time one of the Weebles figures went down the slide. She first had to learn that she had to turn a crank in order to elevate the Weebles figures up the escalator to the top of the spiraling slide, and she had to figure out which way to turn the crank. That only took moments, and once she got the hang of it, she became absorbed in playing with the Weebles Playset. In addition to bringing the happy-faced figures up the escalator and sending them down the curvy slide, one can play hide-and-seek with them (there's a hiding space inside the tree), and one can put the egg-shaped figures on the wobbly tree-house deck. There is lots of motion with this toy to keep a child absorbed.Sometimes after meals and naps she says, "Weebles!" whereupon she RUNS to the Playset. She often dances to the music that plays to "reward" a Weebles figure after it goes down the slide. Speaking of the music, that and the other sounds of the Playskool Weebles Musical Treehouse Playset, such as the crank being turned, is not so loud as to be annoying when compared to some other toys (e.g., a couple of Leap Frog brand toys). My granddaughter's parents, her "nana" (my son-in-law's mom) and I agree on this, though the volume and kind of toy noise a given adult may find overly loud and/or annoying is obviously subjective. This seems to be one toy that will have staying power, and in 16 months my granddaughter's baby brother will be old enough to play with it!Good quality toy; an easy 5 stars and high recommendation. (You can watch a 46-seconds long professionally-made video review of Hasbro's Weebles Musical Treehouse Playset at timetoplaymag.)

reviewText: This is basically a small light box for drawing. There's a small clear part where light shines from underneath - the template sits on top of the shadowbox inside. If the child can trace, this is a fun activity. The box says from age 7, but it's also fun and doable for younger kids, probably from age 4. Perfect for distracting/occupying a child at the doctor's office or at a restaurant.To use it, you need to provide your own 4 AA batteries for the shadowbox. Inside, you can store 20 plastic templates, square papers and a small felt-tip pen. There are little notches on the templates to provide greater stability, but it can pop off if the template is warped. The square paper slides into the slot on top and remains there rather securely.Yes, you can adjust the zoom, but it's very inconvenient because you have to open the green outer box to get to the shadowbox. Also, I wouldn't say it "zooms" because the default setting fills the 4 1/8" by 4 1/8" square paper, and the only change in size is to go smaller.You will run out of paper quickly, so have some extra already cut to fit.

reviewText: I got this for my 7 year old daughter who loves art.  She spends a lot of time drawing and coloring and she loves stencils.  This was something different for her as she can make it one big picture in patterns.  I was a little confused as to how it worked, but I didn't mess around with it, I just gave it to her.  A few minutes later I went in to see if she had figured it out and she had!  All on her own she had completed the drawing portion of the picture and was just starting in in coloring it.  I wasn't sure how many different pictures she could do, but she came up with quite a few different ones and I ended up sitting down with her so we could come up with some together.  She found it to be a lot of fun and was busy making pictures for everyone she knows for about four days and then she started getting bored.  But really, it doesn't matter what toy it is, it's only new for so long... I think if we take it out just once in awhile it'll be interesting every time.If I were to have complaints I would say that I wish it had more of the stencils as it just comes with the one and then the tiny one you can add in. All opinions expressed are my own and I was not paid or influenced in any way.

reviewText: In my opinion this is a domino type game. There are 150 cards total in the set, you play with 10 cards, and you draw additional cards if you do not have a card to play during your turn. You can play a card if you can match it to either of the open ends of cards that have already been played. The idea is to keep roads, rails, and rivers continuous. There are cards on which one of them ends, or begins, or continues.My 4.5 year old son and I played this game one afternoon. He easily understood the rules and it was easy for him to play. My son was excited in the beginning, but after about 15 minutes lost interest. I also lost interest quickly.We played on the floor and the game relatively quickly took a lot of space. We would not be able to play it on his small desk or on the coffee table. At some point I had about 20 cards drawn making it difficult to keep in front of me because of the lack of space. I was able to use most of cards quickly in my following turns, but my son did not want to play anymore, so we did not finish the game.I think the problem is that the game is not too exciting and that was making it seem like it was too long. I guess that if you play with more players, the game may be more exciting.
summary: Takes up a lot of space.  Not very exciting for 2.  May be better with more players.

reviewText: I bought this for my 23 month old granddaughter to use with the Melissa and Doug easel. Here is why I like this.1. This comes with four color coded paint bottles, paint cups, and brushes, and a roll of easel paper. One negative review complained about the brushes losing hairs and the easel paper being too thin, but I have not experienced those problems. True, you can't let your child saturate the easel paper with paint without having something bleed through onto the dry board underneath. But that is true for any easel paper. This easel paper works just fine.However, the easel paper is in fact about two inches narrower on each side than the easel. This means that when my granddaughter paints right up to the edge of the paper, she inevitably gets some paint on the dry board. It easily washes off, but just keep that in mind. I am not sure if an easel pad would be the full width of the dry board, which is 23 inches (the easel paper is only 18 inches wide).2. This also comes with 10 pieces of nicely colored chalk that are just the right size and shape (rectangular stem and tapered tip) for tiny hands. The chalk works well and is not excessively dusty as one negative review complains.Another negative reviews questions why there is black colored chalk for a blackboard. But the chalk is actually a dark grey and it shows up just fine on the blackboard. I sometimes wonder whether people every actually try something before complaining about it.3. This comes with only a single blue dry erase marker for the dry board, which marker I decided NOT to use. It works just fine, but it is NOT washable (which is not a defect--no dry erase markers that I know of are), meaning I would not be able to easily wash it off my granddaughter's hands or clothes. Instead I bought a set of 8 colored washable markers for her to use.I can't use the dry eraser to remove the washable colors, but instead just dampen a small (2" x 3") Scotch brite sponge to wipe the colors off, and have a roll of bounty nearby for when I accidentally put too much water on the sponge.True, this is not as convenient as using a dry eraser, but in exchange I can easily clean my granddaughter's hands and clothing, and also don't have to worry if she accidentally drops a marker onto my carpeting.4. Other reviews note that this comes with only one eraser, which works well on the blackboard. It will also work on the dry board if you use dry erase markers. My only critique is that I think this set should have included two erasers and more than one color for people who want to use dry erase markers.Bottom line: This is a quality accessory set for the Melissa and Doug easel or any children's easel.

reviewText: This was definitely my son's favorite present that we gave to him for his 7th birthday, and I can't blame him.  It's definitely a fun toy... but:-- It's huge.  Luckily all the kids enjoy the toy enough that I don't need to really put it away, but I have no idea how it will store when I do need to put it away.  It will not fit on any shelf or fit into any toy bin unless I take it apart first.-- It's loud.  If you need a quiet race track in your house, this is not for you-- unless you are far away from the track.  Even in my kids' playroom, I can hear the toy going a couple rooms away.  My husband isn't as good as tuning out sounds like this, so this is a definite drawback for him.-- Assembly is required, as are batteries (4 D's).  The assembly isn't hard, but it can be a bit time consuming if you have some antsy kids who are really excited about playing with the toy. Note: assembly is made even easier because each track piece has a letter that you match up to the other piece that has that same letter.  This took me a couple steps to realize!-- Lastly, and I'm sure this is specific to our toy, but a piece was missing to fasten one of the loops.  We were going to call the number on the box, but the toy actually works fine without it, so we haven't yet.  Like I said, this probably won't happen to every single purchase of the track, but it's something I figured I'd mention.Some of the positives:-- FUN.  It is very easy for this toy to hold my kids' attentions (ages 7, 4 1/2 and almost 2).  It's fun to watch the cars go around, and it is especially fun to do multiple cars on the tracks and watch them crash.-- You can "control" the loops to an extent by some knobs and levers.-- More than one car can run on the track at a time.  You will have crashes, but that's part of the fun.-- The track doesn't seem to be too specific about the type of Hot Wheels you use.  We've had one track where you have to pick a certain shape car, but this one will work with lots of our cars.-- It's so easy, my 22 month old can easily work it.  He knows how to turn it on, manipulate the tracks and get the cars to go, and he has a fabulous time doing it.We haven't even attempted using an ipad and the corresponding app.  It really isn't needed.Seriously, if this toy was a bit quieter and easily disassembled or compact enough to store somewhere, it would definitely be one of our top toys.
summary: Great for fans of cars and roller coasters and crashes

reviewText: We've had a few different Air Hogs vehicles in our home, and while my husband and I usually obsess over them, my son will play with them for awhile and then forget about them (unfortunately!) He's 11, now, and I'm learning that the older he gets, the more difficult it is to entertain him. The Air Hogs Battle Tracker, however, definitely did so!PROS- A number of different ways to play. You can either play with two people, one person controlling the helicopter and the other controlling A.R.T. (if you didn't see ART stands for Automated Robotic Turret) with the controller that pulls out of the back. Or, if you're alone, you can play single player, as A.R.T. can be FULLY AUTOMATED. Yes, FULLY AUTOMATED. And yes, it does seriously work. Granted if you're flying around a bit like a maniac (like I may have been...ahem), it takes a milisecond to catch up, but if you're actually trying to attack A.R.T., as you're supposed to, A.R.T. does an amazing job tracking your helicopter!- Let me say it again - AUTOMATED! I never thought I'd see the day when my children got to play with something that is so intelligent. A.R.T. truly is smart as it is able to track the helicopter, and to fire, all on it's own. If it gets hit, A.R.T. proclaims that it has suffered "catastrophic damage" and shuts down (just turn it off and on again to get it started once more). Considering that the little discs that hit A.R.T. honestly don't hurt it leaves me to think that the sensitivity on the turret must be pretty high!- Not easy to damage! One of the things that I've always loved about the Air Hogs products is that they're difficult to damage. It can take some time to figure out how to fly these helicopters (although this one seems to be a bit easier than the others we have in the house), and you should always expect some crashes. Fortunately, even though I crashed it a few times (okay, okay, 15, jeez who's counting), the machine was still working beautifully!CONS:The only real con I have with this toy is the fact that you have to charge the helicopter with the remote. Now this is standard for a lot of Air Hogs items, but it can be frustrating as you have to wait quite awhile for the charge, and you run out of batteries pretty quickly. The A.R.T. has 6 AA batteries, and the remote takes 4 AA batteries, meaning that you're burning 10 batteries for both items. If the company could come up with rechargeable batteries for both units, that would be amazing, but a short-term answer is to simply use some high quality rechargeable AA batteries. (I recommendSanyo NEW 1500 eneloop 8 Pack AA Ni-MH Pre-Charged Rechargeable Batteries- I'm a photographer and these are the only ones I use for my flashes as they hold their charge beautifully - much, MUCH better than regular AA rechargeable batteries!)THE VERDICTYES, YES, YES. This toy gave us hours of play time and what was even better was to see my son and my 8 year old daughter playing together! The only argument they had was who got to run the turret and who got to run the helicopter. Air Hogs you get an A+! This is sure to be THE toy to get for boys this holiday season!
summary: Going to be THE Toy This Holiday Season

The A.R.T. has 6 AA batteries, and the remote takes 4 AA batteries, meaning that you're burning 10 batteries for both items. If the company could come up with rechargeable batteries for both units, that would be amazing, but a short-term answer is to simply use some high quality rechargeable AA batteries. (I recommendSanyo NEW 1500 eneloop 8 Pack AA Ni-MH Pre-Charged Rechargeable Batteries- I'm a photographer and these are the only ones I use for my flashes as they hold their charge beautifully - much, MUCH better than regular AA rechargeable batteries!)THE VERDICTYES, YES, YES. This toy gave us hours of play time and what was even better was to see my son and my 8 year old daughter playing together! The only argument they had was who got to run the turret and who got to run the helicopter. This is sure to be THE toy to get for boys this holiday season!

reviewText: The premise of the Magic Jinn is simple. You think of an animal, and it asks questions (aloud). You answer, and eventually, it makes a guess. There have been other products like this, of course, but this one allows you to speak your answers. Operation is simple. Press the nose of the Jinn (which from the front looks a lot like a cat), and the game begins.The first animal I thought of was a tarantula, and the Jinn never got the answer, though it did guess a wood louse, a centipede, and a cricket. It might have been that one of my answers misled the Jinn. It asked whether the animal was an insect, and I said no. Does the Jinn think spiders are insects?The second animal I tried was a cat. I thought something more obvious would be easier. Again, though, I wondered whether I misled the Jinn. It asked me whether the animal's name begins with F. I said no. Later, it asked if the animal was a feline. Oops. I suppose that does begin with F.The third animal I tried was a hedgehog. Again, the Jinn never got the answer, although it did at one point guess a tarantula. Among the questions it asked were size questions (Is it bigger than a football? No. Is it bigger than a computer mouse? Yes. Is it bigger than a microwave? Yes.--You can see redundancy.) It asked about the animal's diet, whether it's found mainly in South America, whether it's found mainly in Africa, and whether it begins with the letter P. After a few minutes and guesses of chihuahua, chinchilla, mongoose, and tarantula, it gave up.I'm not sure of the suitability of this tow for children toward the lower end of the recommended age range (which goes down to 6, according to the description on this page). Certainly, I can't see children that young knowing the answers to some of the questions. Then again, "I don't know" is always a possible answer. I should add that its voice recognition worked every time with my answers. (You can tell because of the sound the Jinn makes after particular responses.)

reviewText: I've always known Ravensburger to be a producer of excellent, high-end jigsaw puzzles but recently learned that they also have an impressive line of games, arts and crafts, and science learning projects. In fact, the German-based company sells some 8,000 different products worldwide.One of the science learning products is a fascinating forensic science learning toy called "CSI: Crime Scene Investigation" that features 12 different activities for budding detectives ages 8 and older. The kit includes such crime investigating tools as a measuring tape, tweezers, safety glasses, a packet of plaster, evidence gathering bags, a tube and a pipette, fingerprint cards a funnel, and more.One interesting activity allows the young detective to actually isolate the DNA of an apple by cutting it into small pieces, adding it to liquid soap and salt and a special chemical, blending it, and then pouring it into a tube to see the DNA separate from the mixture. Because of the use of chemicals in some activities, such as this one, adult supervision is recommended. The activity involving fingerprinting also is very good. Another is a puzzle solving activity involving phones taken at the scene before and after the crime and another fun activity involves examining tire tracks.The kit does require participants to read a lot so if you child does not enjoy reading they may lose patience. One of the informative passages children can read is a full page devoted to real life German crime biologist Mark Benecke.Because of the high value of this learning toy you will spend more for it but shop around for a good deal. I found prices to differ by $20. Because the price will range from $45 to $65, though, you will want to gift this for a special child in your life. And I'm pretty sure he/she will absolutely love it!

reviewText: What is Mental Blox? It's a memory game, or a critical thinking challenge, or a stacking toy, or a game to learn to follow verbal instructions, or a building set, or a lesson in shapes and colors, and that probably does not even cover all the possibilities.Included are 20 double sided laminated Activity/Question Cards, A Guide, and 20 lightweight, hollow plastic blocks with various shapes, colors, and patterns. The box allows for easy storage and since the shapes are all plastic they can easily be cleaned up after use (a great plus in a classroom!).I got this originally thinking it would work great in one of my special ed classrooms (high school age) since it had a wide variety of play possibilities and potential difficulty levels that could be enjoyed by students with various learning and/or physical disabilities, with ease.I was checking it out when my daughter came by to visit, and she and her friends thought it would be fun to challenge each other (they are in their twenties!). They played for quite a while, using the game where they attempted to memorize and replicate what was on a card after having only 10 seconds to commit it to memory. It was a lot of fun, and she wanted to take it to keep at her apartment to challenge other friends.So, there you go! Mental Blox can be used in so many ways that it appeals to all ages and abilities. My only downside? The cost seems a bit high for a box of plastic blocks...but the concept and design make it so versatile that it's probably worth every penny.I definitely recommend it for the classroom, and my daughter has proven it's great for all ages at home too!

reviewText: I chose this playset for my 3 year old daughter.  She is a huge horse fan, so I knew she'd enjoy it.  I was right.  She really loves playing with the unicorn.  The wings can be flapped and she really likes putting shoes (you get 4 blue ones and 4 purple ones) on the unicorn.  In addition, she likes the hair barrettes.  This set also comes with a cape (hard to put on because you have to get it under the wings and also secure it closed - parents need to do this because little fingers aren't dexterous enough), jewels that can be used to decorate the cape, two tiaras (I need to help my daughter with the tiara), a little plastic hair dryer, a telescope, a treasure chest, two sets of books, and a miniature perfume bottle.  Accessories are cute but they don't all fit in the treasure chest or the drawer in the vanity in the palace.  We are using a little box that we have for storage.  Otherwise, the numerous small pieces will get lost.The crystal palace itself requires assembly.  It comes in a few pieces that snap together and you have to add a few stickers.  It doesn't feel very secure. Also the playset doesn't add much to the play.  It comes with a few hangers, but nothing really hangs on them.  The vanity has a small drawer, but it isn't big enough for storage.  There is a ramp to a second level, but the pony barely fits on the second level of the palace and there isn't much to do.The best part of the set is the unicorn because her wings flap.  The shoes are great too and easy for a three year old to manage, as is the little hair dryer and telescope.  Everything else requires a bit more dexterity that an older child would have (e.g., ages 6+) but this set doesn't engage older children as much unless they are die-hard MLP fans (my older girls are not).Overall, it's cute but could definitely be better.

reviewText: i can't think of any other game like this, but it's kinda like Carcassonne (laying down tiles) blended with Ticket to Ride (laying down tracks)in order to capture the most point value in stones.we played a 3 player game where each of us had 1 goal area where one gains a stone without sharing the gain & a 2nd goal area where u share a gain with 1 other player (6 goal areas total).  the blue & 5 green stones are on the center tile & the yellow stones are along the edge.  the playing tiles have 3 paths on them that connect to other tiles & the object is to move the center stones or the edge stones to one of your goals by placing 1 tile per turn to move the stone further towards your goal.  a secondary motive is to place tiles to derail a stone from an opponent's goal or to block their path.blue, green & yellow stones have different score values & the player with the most stones with the most point value is the winner.it's fun to move the stones around but also try to block your opponents as well.  the game plays in about 30-40 minutes.  it is simple yet the randomness of the tile drawing will keep this game fresh.

reviewText: My 4 year old daughter had a solid 15 minutes worth of fun in the tub with this blue goo.  My five-year old son would not go near the stuff - he found it "disgusting".I followed the directions and put approximately 2 inches of water in the tub, added the blue goo powder, and mixed.  My daughter helped mix by wiggling all over the place - she really had fun with the stuff. As far as cleanup goes, it was a snap - I just dumped the enclosed salt packet into the blue slurry, mixed, waited until it had thinned out, and washed it down the drain. I would not, however, use this product in a tub that drains slowly - the goo will potentially clog a partially obstructed drain pipe.I did, however, have a little trouble getting the goo out of her hair, albeit not too much trouble. This is a novelty item, pure and simple.

reviewText: There are four games in this box.  The four games are King of the Castle, Tasty Bones, The Bird's Nest, and Garden party.  My granddaughter is currently three and a half years old, our target audience for these games.  We played these games a couple of times and there were clear favorites.Garden Party:This game is probably the easiest to understand and was clearly the favorite.  The game is easy to understand and play and the pieces have bright colors.  Each player has five different flowers on their portion of the board.  Each person rolls a die in turn.  If the color on the die matches a flower, then that player gets to put a flower piece on the board.  If they already have that flower, then the next player rolls the die.This game goes very quickly, taking minutes to play.  This game is easy for very young players to understand and win, and my granddaughter wanted to play it after being away from it for a while.  I was moderately surprised that this game was easier for my granddaughter to play than The Bird's Nest, considering this game is recommended for ages 4 and up and The Bird's Nest is recommended for ages 3 and up.The Bird's Nest:This game is recommended for ages 3 and up and is another easy to understand and play game.  Each person chooses a path and places their playing piece on the white starting square.  You may only move forward by rolling the color next to you.  If you roll white, you move forward one square.  Once a player gets next to the nest, it takes a white die to move into the center.  This game is about as fast as Garden Party and generated a lot of laughter in the under 5 set, but seemed a little less exciting than Garden Party because there is nothing to collect or match.King of the Castle:This game is recommended for ages 4 and up, and was a bit of a challenge to play because the rules are somewhat complicated.  Each player rolls the die in turn, moving forward to the next color rolled.  If a player rolls a white, then they choose a "chance" card, which determines where the player moved, either forward or reverse.  If you land on another player's space, then that player needs to go back to the beginning.  When a player gets near the end, if the color rolled is not in front of the player, the player has to go backward to that color.The complexity of this game was a bit puzzling for a toddler.  How do you explain to a toddler that you have to go backward because the color rolled is behind you rather than in front of you, which happens near the end?  How do you explain that landing on another person's space causes a player to return to the beginning?  While achieving this level of understanding and mastering the competition aspects of this game are valuable skills, after all, life is a competition, learning these skills, particularly at a very early age, can be a challenge.Tasty Bones:This game is recommended for ages 5 and up, and was the least favorite game.  No one wanted to play this game twice, opting instead for either Garden Party or The Bird's Nest.  The point of this game is to gather as many bones as possible.  Movement is accomplished by rolling a die and moving to the color shown along any straight, not diagonal, line.  If a white is rolled, then the player moves to the closest white square with a bone card.  However, sometimes it was very difficult to get the colors necessary to gather more bones, and the frustration level grew with time to the point where the game became boring.  There was also a sense that the game was a bit unfair because certain players seemed to have incredible streaks of luck and the outcome of the game might be decided within a couple of minutes, but it could take 10 or 15 minutes to complete the game.Durability:Everything is made of cardboard, except the die.  I suspect pieces of this game will disappear soon, under furniture or in the couch, which will decrease the enjoyment of this game.Summary:Two of these games were favorites, and two were not.  Considering the cost of "4 First Games," it seems to me that having only two games as favorites makes them less valuable than they could be.  There are other games, such as Candyland, that appear to be more fun.  Yes, Candyland and other games take longer to play and are single games, but the enjoyment factor seemed higher.Some parents and grandparents decry the lack of cooperation in these games.  However, while cooperation is also an important life skill, there are other places to teach cooperation, such as doing chores around the house, playing with toys, or in team sports.  When our toddler won the two games she liked to play, she seemed quite thrilled.  She was also happy when anyone else won and for the games she understood and liked, she was ready to play again.The bottom line is that these games are a mixed bag.  Two were fun for everyone.  One (Tasty Bones) was frustrating and boring, and one was somewhat fun (King of the Castle), but some of the rules were difficult to explain or comprehend and this game was not preferred for replay.Good Luck!

Each person chooses a path and places their playing piece on the white starting square. If you roll white, you move forward one square. Once a player gets next to the nest, it takes a white die to move into the center. This game is about as fast as Garden Party and generated a lot of laughter in the under 5 set, but seemed a little less exciting than Garden Party because there is nothing to collect or match.King of the Castle:This game is recommended for ages 4 and up, and was a bit of a challenge to play because the rules are somewhat complicated. Each player rolls the die in turn, moving forward to the next color rolled. If you land on another player's space, then that player needs to go back to the beginning. When a player gets near the end, if the color rolled is not in front of the player, the player has to go backward to that color.The complexity of this game was a bit puzzling for a toddler. How do you explain to a toddler that you have to go backward because the color rolled is behind you rather than in front of you, which happens near the end? How do you explain that landing on another person's space causes a player to return to the beginning? While achieving this level of understanding and mastering the competition aspects of this game are valuable skills, after all, life is a competition, learning these skills, particularly at a very early age, can be a challenge.Tasty Bones:This game is recommended for ages 5 and up, and was the least favorite game. No one wanted to play this game twice, opting instead for either Garden Party or The Bird's Nest. The point of this game is to gather as many bones as possible. If a white is rolled, then the player moves to the closest white square with a bone card. However, sometimes it was very difficult to get the colors necessary to gather more bones, and the frustration level grew with time to the point where the game became boring. There was also a sense that the game was a bit unfair because certain players seemed to have incredible streaks of luck and the outcome of the game might be decided within a couple of minutes, but it could take 10 or 15 minutes to complete the game.Durability:Everything is made of cardboard, except the die. I suspect pieces of this game will disappear soon, under furniture or in the couch, which will decrease the enjoyment of this game.Summary:Two of these games were favorites, and two were not. Considering the cost of "4 First Games," it seems to me that having only two games as favorites makes them less valuable than they could be. There are other games, such as Candyland, that appear to be more fun. Yes, Candyland and other games take longer to play and are single games, but the enjoyment factor seemed higher.Some parents and grandparents decry the lack of cooperation in these games. However, while cooperation is also an important life skill, there are other places to teach cooperation, such as doing chores around the house, playing with toys, or in team sports. When our toddler won the two games she liked to play, she seemed quite thrilled. She was also happy when anyone else won and for the games she understood and liked, she was ready to play again.The bottom line is that these games are a mixed bag. One (Tasty Bones) was frustrating and boring, and one was somewhat fun (King of the Castle), but some of the rules were difficult to explain or comprehend and this game was not preferred for replay.Good Luck!

reviewText: This is a pretty good way to introduce preschoolers to the exciting world of board games. There are four different games in the box, each pretty simple to play. The games require no reading skills, just the ability to match colors. The games included are as follows:"The Bird's Nest" - This one is my daughter's favorite of the four games. Players move up the colored path in the various birds' nests in an attempt to be the first to reach the eggs that are nestled in the center of the nest. This game has two variations of play, one easy variant and one easier variant for those children who get frustrated easily."Garden Party" - Each player has a flower bed and throws the colored die to determine which color flower that player will receive in his/her garden. The first player to collect one flower of each color wins the game."King of the Castle" - For moms and dads who are already familiar with children's board games, this game has a slight "Candyland" flavor to it, except with a castle theme instead of a candy one. Players throw the colored die and move their piece to the corresponding colored space. When a player throws the color white, that player picks a card and moves to the space with the corresponding picture on it. Here is an opportunity for a child to be forced to move backwards, if the picture on the card happens to be located behind the player who drew the card. Of course, the player might also have the opportunity to move forward as well but I thought it was worth mentioning, as this could frustrate the youngest players."Tasty Bones" - Of the four games, this one is our least favorite. The concept is cute...roll the colored die and then move either up, down, left or right to that particular color on the board. When a player rolls a white on the die, that player gets to collect a bone card, provided that player can move to a white space on his or her move, and if there is a bone card on that white space. We've played this game twice and it just took us a very long time to roll a white and collect the bone cards. We spent a lot of time just moving back and forth to different colored spaces on the board. This frustrated my daughter, so we don't play this game anymore.Overall, we enjoy this set of games. These games are made by Ravensburger, which means they are some of the highest quality games on the market.

reviewText: We have a huge water oak in our backyard, with a big, fat, level branch about 30' up.  I rented a cherry-picker from a local big box hardware store chain (think orange), hung chains from it, and then hung this swing from the chains.  Our 18 month old *loves* this swing.  The cross-bar swings up between the legs and sits across her torso, and the shoulder straps snap into place on either side.  Note that the release for the straps is via pressing a latch, and there is a cover over the latch such that you can only put your finger up under it and press the latch when facing the swing, meaning that your child can't easily reach down and release the straps by themselves.All in all a very solid and safe-feeling swing.

reviewText: Best ages: 3-5Batteries required: 3 "AA"PROS:- Comes with about 30 cards with assorted alphabet/math problems (they fit into card holder on his back - good idea, but they don't stay well and are exposed (can get bent)- Activates by button on top of head, will ask child to find a card (like with a string instrument on it) and then once a card meeting those specs is inserted, he will praise the child- Face lights up and will reflect things from the cards (like letters and numbers on the screen) or will be eyes - also the face is used to make expressions (happy, sad, surprised) in correlation to cards that deal with emotions.- Buttons are large and easy for toddlers to press- Carry handle on top (would be better if it moved)- You can purchase additional booster packs of cards if yours bend/break or you get bored or want to focus on more advanced math and reading skills.- Most important: The cards provide an interactive way for your child to learn - Alphie will ask a question, like can you find a triangle - and you child has to look, listen and respond. The voice is syrupy-sweet, downright cloying.As many other reviews have mentioned, it's also extremely sensitive. The lightest touch makes the puppy start singing or talking. (However, for the people who like this toy except for the fact that it'll randomly start singing in the middle of the night, there is a physical off switch under the shirt in the back. Turn it off at bedtime, and your problem is solved.)Lastly, the reason i've taken this toy away even though it has no batteries anymore: New York Public Interest Research Group found that this toy has high levels of bromine and low levels of mercury, both toxic. I didn't like seeing my kid hug and chew on this toy knowing it contains toxic elements.

reviewText: Two nieces, one nephew and I opened the "People At Work 40 Pieces Puzzle Ball" and we conquered it!The kids and I love to do things together and while my nephew is a bit older than the suggested ages he always likes to jump in and help his younger sisters out with tasks such as this. The pieces are extremely kid friendly and very sturdy. I mean, kids of all ages can be pretty hard on toys sometimes and there was no problem with this product standing up to three kids rushing to see who could find more pieces to match first.The thing that was fun for them was seeing the final product once we put the two half circles together to create the "Puzzle Ball".One thing that I liked about the puzzle itself is that you have two ways to construct it. Using the image on the outside of the ball, or on the back of each piece they are numbered. I liked this for my niece who's a bit older who's used both ways to assemble the ball a few times now.In the end, this has turned out to be a hit. I've even shared it with my cousin's kids who have also enjoyed it. I'm excited to see other puzzles from this company with different images. I think these will be the perfect birthday and Christmas gifts to come.

reviewText: My baby is three months old, so he is a little young for this toy but it was so cute that we had to get it early. Still, we really like it. It has a lot of different options and combinations. It offers two modes, letters and music, since my baby is so small, music makes more sense for him. The functions are simple yet well thought and it has an awesome light show, though I am surprised to see my baby likes the simpler and the less glowy things much better, such as the rattle on the fish (it has a transparent tank and it is full of tiny, colorful balls that make noise and spin around) and the guitar (it makes a rattle-like sound when you spin the handle), so most of the time, I just keep it off and just use it like that. I assembled the table and put on the side- the legs act as support and it stays facing the baby so he can see it while he is on his play mat, since he usually looks to the sides more than up, it is a lot of fun for his to look at. Mommy also sits his on his lap and shows his what the different things do and he seems to really enjoy it. I love the colors and the lights are really nice, not excessively bright and shine in a bazillion different sequences depending on what you hit.I can't wait till he can sit up and play with it on his own, since you can remove the legs and just put it on the floor it is perfect for a sitting baby. Later on you can attach the legs and it will help a baby that is just starting to stand up. The guitar seems kind of hard to handle for a little one but all the rest can be just pounded and they will produce an entertaining result, what more can a kid want?Maybe I would like it better if it was not made in China.Overall, recommended.
summary: Fun even for the youngest babies

There are so many subtle colors and intricate reflections, that it was quite a challenge to try to sort out the interior pieces by color and pattern.  In some areas I had to resort to sorting by shape so I could find enough pieces that fit together so I could determine where they fit in the overall pattern.I waited until the entire puzzle was completed before allowing myself to enjoy the glow-in-the-dark view.  Since it was an especially challenging piece of work, I was thrilled to have a special treat on top of the completed puzzle.  An extra bonus is that the individual pieces are very sturdy, so it will survive far more rounds than the average puzzle.

One Polly Pocket doll is included. There are also a number of tiny, plastic accessories that will most likely end up lost. But until then, a storage compartment is included under the play set.I'm sure my daughter will enjoy this toy for a long time and it will totally be worth the hassle of assembling it. Connecting, wall mounted sets are available, too.

reviewText: The premise of this game is simple: you look at a picture on the card and position your blocks to match the picture. There are two sets of cards, so you can choose the easier version (and they're REALLY easy, perfect for a 4-year-old), or a slightly more complex version (which even young kids can do after they've gotten the hang of it). I appreciated its suggestions for different types of gameplay, like:* Race to see who finishes first* A non-competitive "everyone build it!" approach* You can give the younger child the easier set of cards, while the older child (or parent) uses the more difficult set* The older child or parent can create the same object, but is restricted to building with only one handIt was fun and challenging, and my kids played it for days. They haven't sought it out lately (it's been a couple of months), but as a parent I'm inclined to find it so I can encourage them to play it again, because they do enjoy it,and it develops their spacial skills.
