reviewText: Funny Bunny is a simple & entertaining game that should appeal to little ones and which manages to be fun for parents & older kids too.  The gameboard is a plastic hill with a spiraling path of spots leading to the center, where a protruding carrot awaits and marks the end of the path - and victory for the first player whose bunny gamepiece reaches it.  This carrot also serves another purpose, as it can be twisted to open up spots on the gameboard.  If your gamepiece has landed on the spot that opens up with the twist of the carrot, it falls through and disappears from the board and is eliminated from play.  This unique means of eliminating player pieces is what puts the "fun" in Funny Bunny.Gameplay is simple, with each player taking turns drawing a card which either advances that player's piece forward 1, 2, or 3 spaces or which has the player give the carrot a twist.  The suggested age range of 4+ is appropriate, though we've found that on those occasions when we play this to include our almost-four-year-old daughter in playtime the rest of the family enjoys it too, including 7 year old big brother and mom and dad.  Twisting the carrot and anticipating which bunny will drop through the hole and out of sight is actually quite enjoyable.  There isn't much strategy involved, though players have a small amount of decision-making in choosing which of their own 4 bunnies to move during their turn.  Little ones will use basic skills like turn-taking and counting, and will also use a bit of their motor skills when twisting the carrot.Overall this is a cute game that little ones will enjoy and which provides some fun for the older members of the family too.  Make no mistake - this is a simple game aimed at young kids, but the novelty of the disappearing bunnies is clever and gives this one broader appeal than other games aimed at preschoolers.  The board and pieces are cute and sturdy too, and I expect they'll last through as many kids as you need them to.  Overall a fine choice for gaming families that want to include their preschoolers and offer some fun to the older players too.
summary: Cute & Fun for the Younger Set
filteredReviewText: Funny Bunny is a simple & entertaining game that should appeal to little ones and which manages to be fun for parents & older kids too. The gameboard is a plastic hill with a spiraling path of spots leading to the center, where a protruding carrot awaits and marks the end of the path - and victory for the first player whose bunny gamepiece reaches it. This carrot also serves another purpose, as it can be twisted to open up spots on the gameboard. If your gamepiece has landed on the spot that opens up with the twist of the carrot, it falls through and disappears from the board and is eliminated from play. This unique means of eliminating player pieces is what puts the "fun" in Funny Bunny.Gameplay is simple, with each player taking turns drawing a card which either advances that player's piece forward 1, 2, or 3 spaces or which has the player give the carrot a twist. The suggested age range of 4+ is appropriate, though we've found that on those occasions when we play this to include our almost-four-year-old daughter in playtime the rest of the family enjoys it too, including 7 year old big brother and mom and dad. Twisting the carrot and anticipating which bunny will drop through the hole and out of sight is actually quite enjoyable. There isn't much strategy involved, though players have a small amount of decision-making in choosing which of their own 4 bunnies to move during their turn. Little ones will use basic skills like turn-taking and counting, and will also use a bit of their motor skills when twisting the carrot.Overall this is a cute game that little ones will enjoy and which provides some fun for the older members of the family too. Make no mistake - this is a simple game aimed at young kids, but the novelty of the disappearing bunnies is clever and gives this one broader appeal than other games aimed at preschoolers. The board and pieces are cute and sturdy too, and I expect they'll last through as many kids as you need them to. Overall a fine choice for gaming families that want to include their preschoolers and offer some fun to the older players too.

reviewText: My almost four-year-old daughter loves this set.  She wanted me to put it together the minute she saw it, and she's played with it a lot since.  The colors are bright and attractive, the trains are a little bigger than Thomas trains and they fit nicely into her hands, and the trains seem to derail less than the Thomas set she plays with at the library.This set - a "starter" set, is a fairly simple figure eight design with seventeen track pieces, two trains (I also purchased two additional trains), a signal light (which doesn't actually light) and a clock tower and bridge tunnel which can either be stacked or used separately.  My daughter can put the track pieces together by herself, but she can't come up with the figure eight configuration on her own.  Once together, the pieces interlock and stay together nicely.  As the name "starter set" implies, this set is designed to work with other Chuggington railway sets such as the roundhouse and the chug wash sets, none of which are cheap, but if you're willing to spend the money, your child could have quite the toy railroad empire.This toy doesn't really come with a lot of bells and whistles, so the play will have to come from your child's imagination.  So far that hasn't been a problem for my daughter.  I am already looking at other Chuggington sets to get her for Christmas.  The wooden pieces are sturdy and the trains are solidly constructed, so this toy will last for years to come.Unless your child is absolutely set on Thomas, I think this set is a better value and a better fit for preschool hands.  And I definitely recommend it over the Melissa and Doug set.  I just wish it wasn't made in China, but then, they all are.

reviewText: LeapFrog makes some very good toys for children who are beginning to develop language skills.  The Fridge Phonics Magnetic Letter Set may not be the best of their offerings, but it's also not without merit.The set consists of 26 letter shapes and a player (about the size of a handheld radio).  All of the pieces contain strong magnets to keep them securely fastened to your refrigerator.  When your child presses one of the shapes into the player, it plays a short tune listing the letter and what sound it makes.  If the player is activated without a shape in place, it plays the ABC song.Our son enjoyed playing the music and singing along with the ABCs.  The biggest benefit that we received was by using the letter blocks to play "can you show me which letter is. . ."  This sort of reinforcement really helped out when he was learning his alphabet.However, as others have already mentioned, the playset doesn't expand beyond individual letter sounds.  For example, there's no way of playing back how letter combinations sound, and there is no functionality for spelling short words as with other similar toys.  Also, as your child gets older, he/she may want to spell out short words or names - it will then become frustrating when the set's limitation of one-of-each-letter sets in.For these reasons, this is the first baby/toddler toy that I've ever seen that has a recommended age that's too high.  I've found that toys typically promise that children can use/enjoy them much earlier than is practically the case.  However, the Fridge Phonics Magnetic Letter Set is the opposite.  It claims to be for children between two and four.  We gave this to our son around 18 months or so and he outgrew what it had to offer well before his third birthday.While I can't say anything bad about this set, I'd recommend either the LeapFrog Discovery Ball (wider age range and more activities) or Learning Hoops (more phonics/spelling capability and counting) toys before trying this one.PROS* Very good for learning letters via repetitionCONS* Very limited phonics capabilities - just single letter sounds* Only one of each letter means that older toddlers won't be able to make many words* Not interesting enough for the quoted age range

reviewText: When Sharpie announced they would have a permanent pencil that could be erased within 24 hours, I thought it was genius.The problem started when I started seeing reviews of the item elsewhere. And then the big one, it doesn't ever really become permanent.  Sure at some point you can still see a little bit on the paper, which apparently is 'permanent' according to some standards body.  But for you and me, it's not.This might have been an ok product if it wasn't hyped up to do something it wasn't, but even then I'd choose a normal mechanical pencil over this any day.

reviewText: I've never played Apples to Apples, so I really have no way to compare this to the original.  My understanding is that more reading is necessary in the original game, so I think I'm happy with this version.My kids are 8, 10, 13, 15 and 16 -- and we are loving this game.  The product description says it works for 3 or more players, only the box says it is for 4-8 players.  I would say that the game does not work well at all with 3 players -- too many hurt feelings in my house anyway.The game seems to work best for us with at least 5 players.The basic idea is that all players have 5 picture cards in their hands.  The pictures could be fairly normal stuff (a picture of the Colosseum, or a misty road, to name two in my hand the last time we played).  The pictures could be fairly bizarre (a guy in a suit and tie leaning over a toilet intently scrubbing it, for example).One player acts as "judge" (and that position rotates around the table, so everyone takes turns doing that) and picks an adjective, from two listed on a "green apple" card.  This is the only reading necessary, so with younger children, the rules can be adapted so they get help with the reading when it is their turn to judge.After an adjective is chosen, each player chooses a card from their hand that they think most illustrates that adjective.The game is a LOT more fun if you have people who are willing to get creative.  A suggestion in the instructions was to "know the judge" and make your stories appeal to THAT judge.  So for my oldest son, using a Dr. Who reference was always a good choice.  Some of my kids are more likely to vote for the most literal "match" while others go for the most creative.The thing I love most is that this is a game that can be played by a wide range of ages.

reviewText: Among my fondest memories of childhood are visits to my cousins. We enjoyed playing outside games in the summer time and table games during the long Minnesota winter evenings.I like to visualize Mom and Dad with my aunt and uncle poring over a homemade wooden game board, while moving peg markers in an early version of Sorry, originally called Parchisi or Parcheesi; a kerosene lamp was the only source of light in the room.As a family we continued the tradition of table games all through my teens. By then we had a store bought Parcheesi board, with the familiar markers similar to those included in this edition of Classic Sorry!It is gratifying to know that another generation is being introduced to the great game of sorry through this Classic edition packaged as my boys remember the game, including the challenge of competition, good sportsmanship, and the exhilaration being the "spoiler" sending a player's pawn home and being the one to say, "Sorry!"  This classic edition includes special rules for Partnership Sorry, Point Sorry, and Sorry for One.Relive the delightful experiences of family nights at home. Add the smell and promise of fresh popcorn and your family will be creating games of tournament Sorry, challenging their siblings and their friends.
summary: Family Tradition Insured - The Great Game of Classic Sorry!

reviewText: We purchased both a Fisher Price Laugh and Learn Table and a LeapStart Learning Table.  The plan was to see which one our daughter (7 months at the time) liked best.  We would keep the one she liked best at home and send the other to Grandma and Grandpa's house.  Here is how the two compare.1.  The Fisher Price table is shorter than the LeapStart table and baby seems to be able to pull up on it at a younger age. Baby can also sit at the Fisher Price table easier because it is lower.2.  Both have stable legs and do not tip over when baby leans up against them or pushes on them. Both have legs that can be removed for floor play when baby can not stand.  (We never used it this way because our daughter was early to stand.)3.  Both have a learning mode with ABC song and counting to 10 song and a musical mode.4.  In the musical mode the Laugh and Learn table plays tunes to familiar children's songs.  It has a traditional feel to the music.  The LeapStart table has music based on the different instruments on the table such as a banjo tune, a sax sound, etc. and it has a jazzier feel to the music.5.  The Laugh and Learn table has a food theme and looks like a set table.  In the learning mode concepts such as color, shapes, texture, manners, shapes, open/shut, empty/full, peek-a-boo, and naming of common items such as apple, blueberries, banana, juice, etc.  The LeapStart table has a musical theme with instruments such as a piano, maracas, sax, violin, and banjo.  In the learning mode concepts include colors, shapes, high, low, on, off, hello, goodbye, etc.6.  On the Laugh and Learn table the parent has to change the mode.  On the LeapStart table the child can change the mode by turning the page on the book in the center of the table.7.  The Laugh and Learn table has a bowl in the center that spins and can hold favorite objects.  The LeapStart table has a small purple door that can hold favorite objects in the indentation underneath the door.As a parent, I like the LeapStart table more.  The music is parent friendly and even after repeated use, it does not annoy adults.  I also like the different musical instruments and musical sounds that are introduced.  That said, my daughter (now 9 months) likes the Laugh and Learn table better.  She likes putting objects like small balls, Cheerios, and her pacifier in the bowl in the center.  She also likes the peek-a-boo napkin with the peas underneath which says "Peek-a-boo.  I see you." when she opens the door.  It makes her laugh. Another favorite is the spoon rattle that can be removed from the table and the alphabet letters that float in the water sealed in the bowl that move around when the bowl spins.  This is her favorite toy.  She does play with the LeapStart table at her Grandparents house now, but her attention span is short with this toy.  She can play with her Laugh and Learn table for long periods of time.

reviewText: Batteries not included. This toy requires 10 AAA batteries. That's a lot of batteries. I also figured out that Duracell batteries work noticeably better than other brands. I had problems at first with the blue car not responding to the remote. I had put Energizer batteries in it. I had put Duracell batteries in the orange car and it worked fine. So I switched the blue car to Duracell batteries and problem solved. Nonetheless, this is a really fun toy. My 9-year old granddaughter and 2-year old grandson are having a blast with the bumper cars. They are easy to operate. The controls are basic and quite simple. For my grandson these bumper cars are the perfect introduction to remote controlled toys. He is learning how to maneuver a remote control device with a fun, easy toy. And of course the sound effects when the guy pops out are hilarious. The cars run great on carpet or tile but they don't negotiate area rugs very well. They don't appear to be very durable either so I discouraged the kids from launching them off the furniture. Also this is not a good outside toy. But again, the kids love playing with them, and our Chihuahua loves to chase them.

reviewText: I played this game with 5 friends ranging in age from 44-60.  They all happened to be Mensan members, too, but that is irrelevant.  I'm sure the manufacturer's target audience is younger than this group, but I think it works fine for anyone from teens on up.  Some of the logos are older and younger players wouldn't know them, but some are also young, hip companies that older folks won't know.We all enjoyed the game well enough but all agreed that the timer was sometimes difficult to use.  It took us several tries to get it to lock into place for the Reveal It cards where you have to stick the card in the slot and let the timer slowly reveal the picture to the group.  I feel like the timer isn't very durable and the Reveal It cards won't be able to be used once it's broken.We all enjoyed the standard Describe It cards the most, and luckily, there seemed to be the most of those.  Draw It cards are always good for a laugh.  Do It is fun, but I'm glad there aren't as many as the Describe It cards.  Reveal It (all play) is fun, but we had issues with everyone crowding around to be able to see the card clearly, and that was after we finally figured out the timer.All in all, I like the game.  I'm a big party-game fan and I'm quite good at logos and brands, so it's right up my alley.

reviewText: I decided to try this out to wrap gifts at Christmas and while it did a good job I don't see huge benefits over a nice sharp pair of scissors. I must admit that the cuts were nice and clean, but I've gotten the same results with a nice sharp pair of scissors.The one advantage I see in this tool over scissors is that the blade is not exposed, so it would be practically impossible to cut yourself. For the same reason, I could also see this tool being useful for younger children that may be helping to wrap gifts or working on arts and crafts.As is the case when using a pair of scissors to glide through a piece of gift wrap I found that I would have to place some pressure around the entry spot and after that the tool would cut through the paper easily. I've also used this tool to clip coupons.The one problem I see with this tool down the line is sharpening the blade. I understand that this only costs about $7, but I can sharpen the blades on a pair of $7 scissors. Also, in some cases where you have to clip off a piece of gift wrap after having most of a present wrapped you'll still need to pull out a pair of scissors.The ribbon curler works well, but just as is the case with cutting the gift wrap a pair of scissors will also do the trick.In summary I would gladly use this tool if it were part of a gift wrap set or came with a package of scotch tape, but I'm not sure I would purchase it separately to cut gift wrap. It does have it's place for younger children that may be cutting gift wrap or other paper, but in the end I would still prefer a pair of scissors.
summary: Does the Job, But So Do Scissors

reviewText: We are always searching for fun, creative toys for our boys to play with.  This one takes the cake!  We have had the 100 piece set for 6 months now, and both my 7 year old and 3 year old play with it daily.  I've never seen a toy capture their imagination for so long.  They've built hotels, car garages, office buildings, spaceships, and more.  They loved it so much we added to it by buying the 30 piece set as well.  Even I like to play along with the magna tiles and help build, although our kids also play a lot on their own.  When we have other kids over, they also like to play with them and we've had friends purchase their own set after seeing them at our house.  This toy is GREAT for fun, creative, imaginative, long lasting entertainment for kids of all ages!

reviewText: Of all the presents my daughter got for her birthday last month, it was the Furby that got the most attention. I was surprised at first, because it was one of those toys that she'd mention now and then, not expressing a whole lot of interest in. Well, here we are almost a month and a half later, and she's playing with her Furby regularly, and always brings him along for trips. I have to admit, this IS a pretty cool toy! It's leaps and bounds ahead of the original model, and does so much more. If this were around when I was a kid, it'd easily be one of my favorite toys.For starters, the new Furby has a better body model than the original. Instead of just moving its ears up and down, this new one can move its "head" to give it more personality in its actions. Furby can dance along to music, changing how it dances to different genres. The most notable difference however, is the LED eyes. All sorts of expressions are visible in the eyes now, including some wacky icons like cows and dogs that show up depending on what the Furby is doing. The more you talk to Furby, the more English he'll pick up. After about two weeks, we noticed a big difference in how he was talking and singing. The big surprise though was seeing that there are different personalities it can have. From crazy to evil to valley girl (or is that just evil 2.0?), the new Furby is full of surprises. Different personality types come and go, and if you don't like one, you can always just reset it to go back to normal. If you've owned a Furby before, you can expect everything that made that toy fun, and much more, this time around. All the Furbish, the singing, interacting with other Furbies, going to sleep when it's not being played with...Hasbro took what was worked with the original and kept those features, only making improvements. Another big selling point is the Furby app. Download the app and you can feed the Furby all kinds of things, getting different reactions out of it.I'm keeping the details about what we like about the new Furby brief because there's still so much that's undiscovered! Just when you think you've seen everything, a new personality comes out, or it will sing along with a song that I wouldn't have expected it to. This is definitely a five star toy in the fun category, but there are just a few small things holding it back from getting 5 stars overall. First, it takes 4 AA batteries. Just like how the old Furbies sucked the life out of theirs, you can expect the new Furby to go through batteries in no time if it's played with regularly. Get rechargeables when you buy one, and you'll be set. The other problem is a minor gripe of mine, and it's that the motor sound when it opens its mouth sounds almost as loud as the original Furby's. I'm no toy designer, but aren't we past noises like this? It kind of distracts from the cute and cuddly nature of the little creature, hearing mechanical sounds from inside every time it moves. The only other problem is a temporary one- it keeps selling out! Just be patient and you'll find one on here or in stores. Honestly, I'm surprised the new Furby has managed to become nearly as popular as the first model!Any child that's interested in the Furby based on what they've seen in commercials is going to absolutely love playing with it. Furby is still cute, fun to play with, and will likely be one of those toys that your kids remember when they've grown up.

reviewText: "Did you ever play Tic-Tac-Toe?""Yeah, of course.""But you don't anymore.""No.""Why?""Because it's a boring game...it's always a tie."That conversation is from the 1983 movie War Games...and it perfectly sums up my feelings on the board game Urban Myth.HOW TO PLAY THIS:It sounds simple enough, the goal is to travel around the city blocks and collect letters with correct answers to questions that are either truths or myths. But it can get confusing pretty quickly.One person is the card reader, which changes after each turn. A question is read, and the other players vote with their Truth/Myth cards. The players advance one square for everyone who guessed correctly. If a player doesn't guess correctly, they cannot move.If no one gets the question right, the card reader moves one space for each incorrect answer. (Confused yet?)If a player gets a question right and the category on the board matches the category being read on the card, the player gets to move AND keep the card. Whoever spells TRUE or MYTH first is the winner.OUR REACTION:First, The Truth/Myth cards aren't very sturdy - they are weaker than the deck cards and have a greater chance to get creased or ripped.Next, it's common with trivia board games to have a goal to reach while moving the pieces around the board...but that doesn't happen here. You keep going around the same bland board over and over in different city blocks, trying to collect letter cards. Moving the pieces feels kind of unnecessary, to be honest.We noticed some of the questions were phrased in such a way that the answer was pretty obvious. For example:"The premier of the ill-fated X-treme Football League was the least-watched event in the history of prime-time network programming."The use of "ill-fated" in the question leans toward a "true" answer. If the question simply said "The premier of the X-treme Football League was the least-watched event in the history of prime-time network programming", that would be more vague and a little harder to guess.We also felt some of the questions were out of place for younger players, such as the ones below:"An Oklahoma City rapist was sentenced to 30,000 years behind bars.""Iranian women are enrolling in American microbiology classes in order to build biological weapons of mass destruction for release in the U.S.""A man known as 'Slavemaster' on the internet has murdered 56 women and is the focus of an FBI manhunt.""Illinois senator Barack Obama is a Muslim radical."And the crown jewel:"Action star Sylvester Stallone's first role as a leading man was in a 1970's porno flick."Finally, the majority of this game (for us, anyway) was spent breaking ties. When two players qualify to keep a letter, the Card Reader draws another card and asks another question until only one person gets the question right. Some of the questions have very obvious answers, so these ties kept happening over...and over...and OVER. Ties could have been broken MUCH easier by including a single die and having the two players choose a number.All in all, this game was okay...it did have some interesting questions and sparked a few conversations, but we got bored very quickly because every other question ended up as a tie.Fun, but for a limited time.
summary: LOTS of ties, some inappropriate questions, and so-so gameplay.

reviewText: My daughter is almost 2 years old and is already very competent with technology. We try to limit her use of it and she doesn't watch any television so this seemed like the perfect compromise. It's small enough and light enough for her to hold during a long car ride. The video quality wasn't the best but better than I expected. She can easily use the touch screen and loves that her face appears in the "login" screen. But I think most of all, she loves having something to call her own, as she's going through the "mine!" phase.But for the price, I would have expected a little bit more. The apps that came with the LeapPad didn't hold her attention for very long. Fortunately there are plenty to purchase and when there is a sale or a coupon, it's not that bad. I just wasn't happy that I had to spend money on it so soon after getting it.Then, there is the battery. Or lack of one. The 4 AA batteries (that were not included, by the way) didn't last very long. I would say less than 2 weeks and she isn't allowed to play with it for more than an hour a day. We ended up having to purchase the rechargeable battery and power cord. Again, I wasn't happy about having to spend more money on the device so soon after getting it.The stylus is a minor annoyance. It isn't really necessary for the apps we use and it doesn't stay in its place. I'm tempted to cut it off. The stickers weren't necessary either. I think the LeapPad looks better as is.All this aside, once I got apps that would interest my daughter and the rechargeable battery, it has been great. She loves it, I love that she stopped asking for my iPad, and we now have something to occupy her on long car rides, after the books and crayons have lost their appeal. It's easy to use and I can see my daughter using it for many years to come.
summary: 2 year old loves it, I have a few complaints

reviewText: Call me a traditionalist, but in most cases I end up disliking board game variations.  The originals became popular because they are fun.  Why toy around with a good thing?  The Monopoly brand has been guilty of this in the past with sometimes downright embarrassing results.  (Did anybody really needPirates of the Caribbean Monopoly?)  It screams MONEY GRAB.In the case of Monopoly Empire, you're presented with a legitimate reimagining of the game that keeps the spirit of the game intact while providing some variations in game play that will appeal to some players even more than the original.The object of Monopoly Empire is to aquire a stable of popular brands (i.e.: Nerf, Hasboro, Ducati, Coca-Cola, etc...).  The first player to fill their office tower with brand tiles is the winner.Similar to the original, the brands vary in value with higher-priced brand tiles being wider, filling your empire tower quicker.  One of the brilliant game play simplifications:  Your tower has increasing value markers - the more tiles you have, the higher your value.  The rent you pay and the amount you're paid when passing GO are both determined by your empire value.  This means no more referring to various property card charts to determine payments.  (My kids were able to grasp this instantly, which makes for much more enjoayable family game play.)Another simplification:  There are only 3 paper bill denominations.  This speeds up gameplay significantly and (again) makes the game much more kid-friendly without dumbing it down for the adults.  (Anyone really enjoy trying to organize your personal bank in the original Monopoly?  I didn't think so.)Adding to the variety and strategy are Empire Cards, which have taken the place of Community Chest cards.  All players begin the game with 2 Empire Cards and can aquire more throughout the game.  They are player-controlled cards that can throw a real monkey wrench into your opponents' plans.  Empire Cards enable one to swap the topmost property with another player, reverse rent payments, block another player's action, and of course, get out of jail free.Even Free Parking has been given a facelift, making it more than just a placeholder space.  For an optional $100,000, one can take a trip to any space on the board.The full-color instructions included with Monopoly Empire are easy to follow and cover most contingencies.  You'll be up and running with this fun game in no time.  Gameplay varies from 20 - 40 minutes, and has great replay value.If you enjoy Monopoly but haven't been able to talk anybody into it (because they think it takes too long or is too complicated), Monopoly Empires is just the ticket for a great game night.

reviewText: We are a family that has (tries to anyway) weekly game nights, so we're always looking for new board games to put into the rotation. Tapple was a huge hit, both for the kids, and adults.The game play is relatively simple. You pick a card that states a general category (e.g. junk food) and then each player has 10 seconds to name one item from that category. The trick is that once you name something that starts with a letter (e.g. chips), you can't use that letter again. Letters are pressed on the wheel to indicate which have been used already. If you can't do it within your allotted (very brief) time, you're out. The round ends when only one player is left standing.The format allows for quick game play: you can make it as short or long as you want, playing for time, or, as we did, the first person to five "points" (a.k.a. round wins). And you can even, pretty easily, make up your own categories, allowing for fairly limitless replay potential and plenty of imagination.Though the ages say 8+, our 6-year-old was able to play this easily, as long as we selected general categories with which he reasonably has knowledge.Great idea and one I'm sure we'll play again and again.
summary: Fun, Fast-Paced and Appropriate for Most Ages

reviewText: I love that this plane is made from 100% recycled materials. The design is interesting - it's a series of large molded parts which snap together - though it's not easy to take apart, it is possible to do so - by an adult with a flat head screwdriver to pry it apart at the connections. Since there are several of the connections which would need to be opened simultaneously, you're going to have to really want to get it open to bother with it.The body of the plane has numerous drainage slots on the underside, but the pontoons have drainage openings on the top - so it will take an adult to do a good job at draining this after water play. That said, it is diswasher cleanable, so I don't see this as too much of a big deal. Haven't had it long enough to see how it holds up, but I suspect, based on the quality and thickness of the plastic, that it has longevity.I think it's a little bit bulky and heavy for a 1 yr old who is still working on grasping things- especially when made heavier by water inside. A 2-3-4 yr old will have a lot of fun with it. The propeller is pretty sturdily designed as well, and spins around. The edges of the blades are certainly rounded somewhat but I would prefer they be even more rounded. The plastic seems to be high-quality, not too thin but not overly thick, either. The drainage openings on the pontoon are small enough to protect little fingers from getting stuck in them.It's a simple, imagination play toy and my grandsons (ages 1.5 and 3+) both enjoy playing with it, though the 3 yr old finds it more interesting. It's a little big for the bath if you bathe two children at the same time, but for a single child, it's acceptable. I think it's better suited to an outdoor pool for waterplay- purely because of its size. But even though it's designed as a water toy, it's nice enough to play with 'dry'.The kids like it, and I think it's a safe and ecologically responsible toy, so I would happily recommend it to anyone with toddlers.

reviewText: Summary: Simon Flash reinterprets the classic Simon game using cross-communicating light squares (they are not quite cubes). The result is intriguing, but the games themselves are not terribly challenging or sufficiently interesting to keep one playing for long.As an electronic game, Simon Flash does not entertain for very long. The first problem is that while the squares are novel and fun to play with initially, the games don't have legs. I'm old enough to remember playing with the original Simon when it came out in the 1970s, and back then the main competition was Parker Brother's Merlin and Coleco's sports games like Electronic Quarterback (the Atari 2600 was in its own class). Simon Flash would have amused us greatly back then, but today the electronic games have become so sophisticated (e.g., iOS games, Nintendo 3DS, etc.) that I don't think many people (and especially kids) are going to be enthralled for long, certainly not like we were back in the dark ages. I can see from watching my own children that they quickly comprehend the device, play with it for five minutes, and then move on. I think even the original Simon had more depth than Simon Flash, as the squares have no difficulty levels and seem to be slow communicating with each other. In fact, I always feel like I'm waiting for the squares to finish speaking with each other. Maybe it is more fun if inebriated (adults only, please).My main disappointment with Simon Flash is that its technical limitations greatly limit the variety of games that you can play. Simon Flash is one of the first mass-market products that taps into an idea that has been experimented with for a while in electronic gadget circles, namely modular objects that cross-communicate (see, for example, Modular Robotics' Cubelets and Sifteo Cubes). Simon Flash is a very simple implementation of this broader idea, though I am sure that it was an engineering challenge to do this economically in a product manufactured by toy factories and sold to children. Simon Flash's squares only communicate with each other properly when they are within about a 1/4 inch of each other, lined-up, and facing the correct direction. How many games can you design using a linear pattern of four squares of four colors, all of which must be oriented the same way? You can imagine how the number of games and puzzles could be increased if the shapes could be arranged in any pattern and with as many squares as you liked (e.g., a 3 x 3 matrix could be used for tic-tac-toe). Indeed, I found one of the most interesting things to do with the game was orienting and reorienting the squares in order to learn the technical rules for their operation. These are intriguing devices, but I find them more suggestive of new possibilities than anything else.Finally, a word about the general design and build quality. One of the game's nice features is the elegant plastic holder that makes for easy storage and transport. You can also play Simon Classic while it is in the holder. I find the build quality of the squares to be merely okay. I don't think they are particularly rugged, and at times the button mechanism required a certain touch in order to register properly (as did all the old electronic games from the 70s!). The programming of the cubes is, for the most part, fairly straightforward.

reviewText: No toy has ever come out of retail packaging so easily.  There were none of those big old wire ties that cut your hands and break your nails  protecting said toy from Armageddon.  Instead of going into my snipping mode, I turned the toy over to see what was involved.  The first two big circles just had to be turned to set one of the doll parts free.  Then there were button like things.  Pull off the tape and then pull the plastic through it.  There were also a couple of ties and then turns that were easy to undo.  Amazing.The box that is salvaged by taking the parts out carefully, leaves a little sort of play house for the doll.  If the doll had a baby it might be small enough to use the table.For the life of me though, this looked like the inside of the Boxcar for the Boxcar children with one pink cup, one spoon...One thing that bothers me is that the doll falls forward when it is in the seat - and it looks like a backpack.  Should we be teaching children to put the baby in their backpack?Another small problem I noticed was that its tricks cause it not to be a cuddly doll.  The middle of it is essentially a hard box.Oh, and for the retail price?  I would not have chosen this one for that price.  I would have selected something bigger.

reviewText: This addition to LeapFrog's Read & Write Series teaches 4 to 8 year olds how to write upper and lowercase letters and recognize letter sounds. It works with LeapReader's separately sold rechargeable, electronic chunky pen,LeapFrog LeapReader Reading and Writing System, Green. The book is a sturdy, spiral-bound, board-like book with bright engaging colors and drawings that tell the story of how a group of stick-figure children put a band together for the community fair. The players in the band represent the sounds of various letters that help the reader learn to sound out words. Each page has fun, interactive learning activities performed with the chunky pen. The audible sounds of instruction, encouragement and praise come from the chunky pen, when placed on specific areas of the pages. Not only does the reader learn to sound out letters, but also how to write them with sequential instructions for each pen stroke.This is an engaging, playful and highly portable way to help children learn to read and write, even in the car on road trips.

This might be the shortcoming of the device, is that different papers need to be cut to fit into the holder.  She was not interested in making the entire circle and didn't really understand turning the wheel around, but she was still very pleased with it.Pros:Well made (has not been broken by a 2.5 and 5 y.o.)Good for different ages and skills.  You don't have to make the complex designs shown.Will grow with them so that someday they will probably want to make the mandalasCons:We had no idea what a Mandala was and had to look it up!If you use different paper than what is included, it has to be cut to fit in the holder. (minor inconvenience)
summary: Fun for drawing, even if you don't follow the directions!!

reviewText: We started with the Melissa & Doug Vehicle Chunky set - and after my son being so in love with it, we had to get a few more.This one is SOOO FUN! As he puts the puzzle pieces in, I'll tell him what the animal is and what noises they make and he tries to repeat (for now at least, when I say Cow, he doesn't say mama). Ha!The puzzle is very sturdy. My son likes to peel off the pictures or rip up the pieces of his previous puzzles, with this - he hasn't succeeded.What I like about this is that the picture is on the board so he just has to match the shape on the puzzle piece and stick it to the board. It's helping him figure out sizes/shapes and fits. I really like this.As for complaints of previous reviewers: I don't expect this toy to be like the ones of olden days where they are hand painted and hand made and blah blah blah. It may last though this kiddos childhood, but I'm not planning on this to last through several generations. It does what I need it to do and for the price, come on, it doesn't get any better.

reviewText: I received this toy thinking it would be great for my three year old son. His eyes lit up as he opened the box and loved the sounds. I did like the fact that the toy offers a volume control which came in handy to say the least.Lets start with quality: The board is plastic and seems very strong, should last. The crane comes off very easy and my little boy has a hard time putting it back on. I am guessing I will have to glue it otherwise it is essentially not usable. I did see that one of my toy's was missing the wheels but it still slides fine. So they clearly have problems in the assembly department of their factory.Usability: though the sounds are great and my boy did figure out to push the buttons there is a while interactive part of the game. Of course the interactive part of the toy is for a little older kids I will admit it took quite a bit of thinking, figuring, and guessing to get it to work (and I am an engineer). The problem is you have to use the instructions to know where to place each vehicle exactly where they should be and understand the buildings purpose noted in the instructions. So in short I don't think a kid will figure it out. I think if they simply labeled on the board where to place the vehicle and labeled the buildings so when it says "go pick up a load at the construction site" ... meanwhile you are thinking this whole board is a construction site ... it turns out one of the buildings is considered to be the 'construction site'.It is a fun little toy and worth a try. I like that the parts are attached accept for the vehicles so there are less pieces to keep together.Happy Shopping!

So, the kind of kid who likes those will probably like the Zoobles, too.

reviewText: I purchased this with high hopes given all the outstanding reviews. Out of the box, I was immediately taken aback by how "wonky" the toy looked. Was it not possible to sew and stuff the toy so it's head is symmetrical? I also found the overall proportions a little strange- designed to look like the picture- ie cute when in the seated position. Not so cute otherwise. Small detail but a minus in my book. My daughter will not notice it but I do.The set up was fairly easy. Download, connect, sync, disconnect. The USB cable is very short but its not a deal breaker, unless your USB port is not easily accessible. You also have to create a "parent account" to get started.Right now my daughter is not really interested in Violet. She loves toys she can do something with (stack, roll, drop, open, shake etc) and sadly Violet doesn't do these things. The 4 paw buttons all have a function, one of them being the power button. The buttons are very sensitive so you may end up skipping though a song you may have been enjoying or simply turning Violet off mid song. The hearts on the tummy is also a button. Your child will have to figure out and remember which button does what- which is good for memory and recollection.They have a huge selection of names and my daughters name (pronounciation but not the spelling) was available. Leapfrog has to work on the inflection of the names though. They all sound like a question.Programming the toy to say your child's name, favorite colour, food etc is definitely a good feature as your child gets old enough to understand those things. Violet does talk a lot so be prepared for a good amount of chatter. Violet talks about colors and animal sounds but I find it somewhat abstract as there is no clear visual to help reinforce what she is saying. The light on the collar flashes but sometimes it's related to what she is saying and sometimes it's not. It's confusing.Talking about hiccups and snuggling- also pointless to me. Perhaps Violet could just try counting to 10 or 100. No hiccups.Violet is a nice toy to have but I don't think it's a must have toy. For a toy designed to be loved by little ones, I am very surprised that it's not washable. You do get your money's worth for the price of the toy. However, if Violet stopped working and I had to buy another, I wouldn't.

reviewText: This toy was such a disappointment. It worked great for the first 15 minutes or so and the kids had a blast, but the batteries quickly ran down and the balls stopped popping out. They would just hover at the tip of the nose. A few minutes after that, the batteries would stop completely. It didn't even matter that we would replace them with high-quality batteries - this thing needs massive amounts of power to work properly, and unless you are willing to spend a small fortune on batteries and replace them almost daily, the toy isn't going to work properly. Another issue is the balls. It only comes with 5, and they are thin and too easily crushed. And of course, the crushed balls won't pop out. You can buy replacement balls for $15 a pack, but that's half the cost of the elephant itself! Ridiculous. My advice would be to save yourself the headache and get some other toy.

reviewText: FIRST AND FORMOST: The only place we could find this item before Christmas was on leadfrog's website and we had to buy a bundle to get it.  If you are having trouble finding a leappad, keep checking their website as I spoke to a rep and they said they should have more soon.I will give my initial impressions and tell you what our expectations are for this toy.  When my daughter gets it for Christmas I will update this review with her impressions and post future updates to provide more info and review details on durability and use.We have 3 kids (2 year old boy, 4 year old girl, and 7 year boy).  All of them have grown up using the leapster that our oldest son received when he was 3..it has given out after a lot of use.  They all are comfortable with using the leapster, iphone/ipod touch, and the computer, so our expectations are that they will be able to utilize the leappad quickly.We bought the LeapPad for our 4 and a half year old daughter.  She is in pre-school now and will be going to kindergarten in the fall of 2012.  She had a lot of trouble learning letters and phonics until this past summer when things began to click, but there is a lot of room for improvement.  We hope she will be able to read simple books by the end of next summer (just before kindergarten). She handles math concepts well for her age and is very creative.  We expect that this toy will excite, encourage, and motivate her to make more strides (with our involvement and direction) as much as the original leapster did in the following areas:SpellingWriting SkillsReading SkillsMath and Logic SkillsDrawing SkillsBasic Camera and Video SkillsI expect this toy to last as long as the original leapster did (at least 4 years) and to be handed down to our 2 year old in 2-3 years.I am also excited to see how it tracks my daughters "learning path" over time.  Hopefully it has some useful information.Packaging was okay...It was shipped in larger box which was not filled very well.  When delivered the leappad and games in the box were bouncing around.  I can only imagine how much bouncing they did between Canada and South Carolina.  However, everything got here safe and appears to be working well.What came in the box:- 2 styluses - both are magnetic and one included a string to attach to the leappad.  I like the magnetic stylus idea, but the string attachment was a nice touch to help to ensure we don't lose the stylus.- CD for installing the leappad connect.  You can also download this software for free from the leappad site.- USB cable for downloading/installing games with leappad connect.  It also allows you to move pictures/movies taken with the leappad camera to the computer.- 4 Apps - Pet Pad, Story Studio, Art Studio, and one you can choose from 5 options online (we chose the jewel train logic game).  Nice touch to allow you to choose the last app imo.I installed the leappad connect on my computer and downloaded the games to the leappad so that my daughter will be able to play with it right away after opening her gift.  It took around 30 minutes and was very intuitive in my opinion.The screen looks great, but is glossy and a fingerprint magnet.  The only concern I have is scratches that are bound to happen when entrusted to a 4 year old :)We purchased a screen protector for it as well.  I STRONGLY RECOMMEND purchasing a screen protector for something like this.  We use them on all of our electronics that the kids use (PSP, iphone, ipod, and DS) and I can't express how well they protect them from scratches and fading from normal use.  I purchased the Lexerd - Leapfrog LeapPad TrueVue Crystal Clear Screen Protector.  They also have one that has a matte finish to reduce glare.  I plan to review that at a later time as well.We also bought the carrying case for the leappad.  It comes in pink and green.  This should help protect it when she takes it on trips and transports it to and from the car and hopefully aids in teaching her to take care of her leappad.  The leapster connect includes a "Skill Selector" section that claims "Some LeapPad games allow you to customize the learning.  You can select the Mathematics skills or Spelling words that you want your child to practice...".  This sounds interesting and useful if it is utilized.  There are quite a few apps (games, books, videos) that you can download as well ranging from 5-20 dollars.It takes 4 AA batteries...I will provide more info on how long they last after Christmas.  We'll probably use rechargeable batteries in the end, but for now we have the regular alkaline batteries.The speakers and volume work well and provide enough sound to be played in a car.  It does have a headphone jack for those times that parents would like it to be quiet.Camera Resolution: Up to 640 x 480Video Recorder Resolution: 320240The bundle we got includes an Mr. Pencil Saves Doodleburg, LeapSchool Reading, and an App Center Download Card (to allow downloading of more apps)Out of the box, I am very impressed with the quality of the leappad and and very excited to see my daughter grow with it.If you have any questions or anything, please add a comment so I can make this review as useful as possible.UPDATE: Nov 30, 2011I received an email today and they gave me a free download code for Alphabet Stew.  This is normally a $7.50 app/game to download.  The email said valid until Dec 15th.  I'm not sure if this happens for anyone who sets there leappad up before the 15th or not.  If this is a Christmas gift for your child, then I recommend that you create an account and register your leappad with the leapfrog connect software.
summary: Initial Review and UPDATES to come

reviewText: *Update, two years later:  Surprisingly, this is still a favorite tool whenever we need to wrap a gift.  The razor has stayed sharp, and I've found myself going to look for it rather than use scissors on several occasions.*I was really skeptical about this cutter, since I figured scissors pretty much do the job when I'm wrapping gifts.  After using this while wrapping a stack of gifts Christmas Eve, though, I have to say I'm a convert.  This light-weight little tool cuts evenly, quickly, and very easily, with no snags or wrinkling of the paper.  Works best cutting away from you, but also works cutting across with a little care.  The paper doesn't have to be completely flat like I expected, and I would say it actually saved some time.  We'll definitely be using this again and again!

But that is a very minor complaint.  Overall I love this thing.

reviewText: I purchased the "Laugh&Learn Crawl Around Car for my great-niece who is a special needs toddler.  Her therapists have recommended toys and games that stimulate her senses without overwhelming her brain.  I am happy to report that this car is truly a hit with her, with her parents and her therapists.  This toddler sized "car"  has all the bells and whistles (literally) of any ride-on toy, and little ones get to "drive" just like mommy and daddy.  The best part about this toy is that it doesn't move!  It is perfect for crawlers, standers and toddlers just beginning to walk. The Car is stationary, making it very easy for a toddler to climb in and out and all around the outside.  There are buttons to push and knobs to turn and shapes to insert, on every part of the car.  Lots of light-up dials and sounds, as well.  Fisher Price has done a great job in understanding what toddlers find "fun" while engaging and stimulating their minds and bodies.  This "Laugh & Learn Crawl Around Car" does exactly what it's name says - my great-niece laughs, crawls around and has learned different skills all while "playing" with this toy.  This toy has been used pretty constantly for over four months with no real signs of wear and tear.  I highly recommend this toy for any young toddler who likes to "drive" but is not quite ready for wheels, yet!

reviewText: I picked this up based on the Scrabble name alone and as you may have already read in other reviews this handheld has little (i.e. Nothing!) to do with the traditional game of Scrabble. This is the simple game of 'what word or phrase am I thinking' and it does the job admirably. It's a team game so your goal is to get your partner to guess correctly without you using any of the desired words. So your aim is not to stump someone - it's to help without 'cheating' then pass it to the next team for their go and as such it only works with a minimum of four people so do keep that in mind.  But that's the fun I think - it's a party game, one to drag out after a few saucy drinks and throw down some word skills for a little while. Which is exactly what we did.The unit itself is much bigger than I expected. I was anticipating something like the little 20Q handhelds but this is about 8-10 inches tall and this aids in its durability and also the larger screen and buttons help.So - a great inexpensive fun guess-the-word game that takes all the scoring chores away leaving you to simply play and have fun with adult(ish!) friends. Enjoy it this holiday season.

reviewText: Jigsaw puzzles are as old as the hills, so it's nice to see them adapted into this fun format.  The puzzle, when completely assembled, is HUGE -- 3 feet X 2 feet.  The ideal place to work on such a large puzzle is a smooth floor.  The puzzle is designed for kids 3 and up, and that age designation is appropriate.  There are only 24 puzzle pieces, so young kids will not get overly frustrated trying to put the puzzle together.  The picture of the wizard and assorted dragons, with a big blue fire-breathing dragon in the center, is striking and should appeal to kids who love fairy tales and stories about knights and chivalry.Since kids often may not have the most pristine of hands, the puzzle pieces are easy to clean.  For parents with imagination, when the puzzle is completed, a story can be made up to match the action in the picture.  If you're used to traditional jigsaw puzzles, you'll be surprised at how gigantic each puzzle piece is, but keep in mind this is designed for little ones, so the larger the piece, the easier it will be to locate its proper place in the picture.These days, there are so many electronic devices to intrigue children -- iPads, iPods, computers, cellphones -- that's it's a pleasant change of pace to see a child playing with a kind of retro pastime, using visual, motor, and problem-solving skills.

reviewText: Players start the game by drawing cards which give them train routes across the US they should aim to create.  During the game, they create train routes, earning points for each segment created, plus bonus points for completing a designated route.  It's a strategy game with a dose of luck.  But compared to Ticket to Ride Europe, it is less cutthroat, and harder to thwart other players.  The game is fairly predictable, but fun and appropriate for both adults and children, groups of up to five as well as two players.  It's also good for those who want exposure to U.S. geography.  A fun, well-made game.  Recommended.

reviewText: I got this game in June and have since played it close to thirty times without any talk of expansions. I've played it with those who aren't familiar with more complex Euro-style board games and with those who are, and the consensus is that this game is fun. It was the big, stand-out hit at both sides of my family's Christmas celebrations.The game is civilization building, and the main mechanism is card drafting. Each turn involves choosing one card from a hand of cards and passing the rest to the player on your right or left. The main enjoyment in this game is the tough decisions. You have to balance choosing a card that will be the biggest help to you with not passing a card to your opponent that will be the biggest help to him with maybe passing a card that won't come back to you later. Each decision is interesting.I also like that this game is in some ways very forgiving. A player ALWAYS has an option on his turn (even if it's just discarding a card for coins), and at the end of the game, everything can score a player points. This usually keeps games tight.Also to 7 Wonders's advantage: up to seven players can play the game, and the game time is almost unaffected in the scale up from three to seven players. And the game is about the same level of fun for three, four, five, six, or seven players. (I didn't care for the two-player variant.)The iconography can be hard for new players to pick up, but after a single game (which takes 30-45 minutes), new players usually won't have problems (and will probably want to play again anyway).I recommend getting the Mayday premium card sleeves for this game, as it will probably see a lot of use and it would be best to avoid uneven wear on the cards.7 Wonders is a fantastic game, and a game in my collection that sees lots of play.

reviewText: OK, this is complicated. If, back when I was 10 years old, someone told me that I could have a remote control helicopter that fires "disks" at a radar tracking station that was automatically following my every move and was capable of shooting missiles at me - and hitting me - I would have said you were CRAZY! But that's exactly what the Air Hogs - Battle Tracker does and it does it for about $100 bucks. If the government had designed this, it would cost $1,000,000, be as big as a tractor trailer and not work worth a darn - but I digress.I ordered this for my 8 year old nephew for his 2012 Christmas present. You should have seen his eyes light up when he ripped off the wrapping paper and saw what he had from Uncle Dom and Aunt Pat! However, the complicated part started immediately when we tried to get the darn thing out of the box. We literally had to rip the cardboard apart to get inside and then I had to use a knife - carefully - to cut the pieces and parts out of the box. Then, there were these twist clips that you had to find an remove to free the toy from its confines. Absolutely not a job for an 8 year old! Next, you had to make sure you didn't toss out the "disks" that the helicopter fires (we did and had to run to the recycle bin to rescue them) and you also have to gather up the missiles that will spill everywhere as you rip the toy out of the package. Then, you need 10 AA batteries and a small screwdriver to load up the power. And then, you have to suss out how to load the missiles. charge the battery in the copter, and then figure out how to fly it. Whew! My nephew just wanted to play with it and kept flying it into the ceiling and then, when it hit, he stopped flying it and it came crashing to the floor. Hmmm! I must have told him (a bright kid and a good reader) 100 times to read the instructions but he just smiled and kept flying the copter until he ran it out of power. I did manage to fire up the tracking station (very cool) and sure enough, it followed the copter's erratic flight path as my nephew smashed it into the Christmas Tree, walls, ceiling, his brother and me. It even locked on long enough to fire a missile (and miss).Honestly, the technology in this toy is simply mind boggling. A remote control copter is flat out cool and a lot of fun. Throw in that the copter fires disks via remote control is icing on the cake. But when you add the tracking station that follows the copter and automatically fires missiles - semi-accurately - through some kind of defense system programming, I'm simply blown away.So - why 4 stars? The first reason is the difficult-to-remove packaging. What a waste - both of time and resources. Next, the thing requires that you both read the instructions to get the most out of the toy (for example, you are warned that you shouldn't recharge the copter for 10 minutes after use so that the battery cools down - like a regular kid will be that patient?). And then, learning to fly the copter is hard. Again, for example the controller has a switch for something called "trim" but the instructions do not explain very well what trim is and how you can / should use it  to improve the copter's flight. Finally, it doesn't fly very long before you have to recharge the copter - from the base unit's batteries, not a wall charger. Talk about frustration - for a kid and for the parent / uncle trying to help the kid learn to enjoy this complex toy. And speaking of charging, if you don't follow the proper charging sequence - turn the copter off, set the base unit to charge, plug in the wire to the copter - your copter won't charge properly. More added frustration there!If you are an adult or a VERY patient pre-teen or teenager, this could be a great present and a toy that could be used without supervision. However for an 8 to 10 year old, it may not be simple enough for the child to get the maximum enjoyment from this amazing bit of 21st century gadgetry.Like I said, it's complicated.

reviewText: This board game has a simple premise - guys ask gals "guy questions" that they have to get right to advance, and vice versa. The questions are ok, but aren't very balanced. Some are ridiculously hard, some are way too easy. While the game is rated for 12 and up, many of the questions are beyond a preteen maturity level. The worst part about this game is that its unnecessarily confusing. The game includes wild cards that differ for each gender, the ability to capture prisoners, multiple game pieces on the board (but you only move one at a time), and a limit of three moves per turn not counting any interruptions from a wild card of your own gender . . . huh?Pros:* The cards/questions are decent. Could be entertaining with a large group of people to just tally your own score with pencil and paper.Cons:* Instructions are very confusing and make the game worse* Board is unnecessary, detracts from the game* Wild cards are an add on that makes no sense* No storage place for the cards (4 decks you have to keep separated)* Not fun without a large groupAll in all, this is an ok game for large groups of people of opposite gender, just don't expect to get anything out of the board or the wild cards. Take turns quizzing each other on "opposite sex trivia" and it will entertain for awhile.

On your turn, you discard cards and move your pieces according to the cards you choose to play. The cards determine your moves on the game board. For example, a pair of cards allows you to place two of your pieces anywhere on the game board. The object is to create a line (or path) of your game pieces from one side of the board to the other side of the board.This is a good game for tweens and their parents. I'd recommend for grades four and up.

reviewText: My kids have a boat-load of Imaginext products. Some we purchased new, some we received as hand-me-downs, and some (like this one) we received as sample products. Since we have about ten Imaginext playsets out on the family room floor at any given time, it's safe to say that we are fans of the product line and can easily compare this new set to what has come before.This (smallish) play set has two main parts: a small blue spaceship and a launch pad. There is one small astronaut figure that comes with the set, but he has no companions or enemies to play with him.  :(  I was a bit surprised by this fact, as well as a bit disappointed. It seems to me that every mid- to large-sized play set should have two character figures included with it. It makes the set more fun to play with - whether a child is playing on his/her own or with a friend. The figure has a removable space helmet, but that really isn't any big deal. It's just one more knick-knack to keep track of. Personally, I would have preferred to have the helmet permanently attached.The launch pad has several moving parts, including docking clamps, a fuel hose, a "transporter" beam, a personnel lift, and a ball turret that shoots a small plastic rocket projectile. Naturally, the astronaut can be placed into the transporter, into the ball turret, or on the personnel lift to load him into the spacecraft.The spacecraft, itself, is pretty small. I would have preferred it to be larger, but my son seemed OK with it the way it is. The clear plastic cockpit canopy can be raised to seat the astronaut inside. The spaceship has several buttons - each of which can be pressed to activate a number of features. One button launches plastic projectiles (the same kind used in the ball turret). One button extends four small, red wings from the bottom of the craft. The last button activates a samll red light on the top of the spaceship, accompanied by sound effects and phrases such as "Alpha Explorer ready to go!" or "Right on target!" or "Time to go home!" The ship's color scheme is blue on top, grey on bottom with accents in red. If placed in an upright launch position it will stand, freely.Personally, I don't like this little set nearly as well as some of my kids' other Imaginext sets, but my youngest son seems to like it as well as or better than the rest of them, and I guess that is the best recommendation I can give it. Most little boys have similar tastes, so if my son likes it, your son probably will, too. I would rate this product as a three-star item if I was grading it based on my own personal opinion. However, since my son would clearly give it a five-star rating, I will average the two and give it a four-star rating.One last thing I should point out: This product IS battery powered and comes with the required batteries necessary to power it. Unfortunately, the included batteries in my unit were DOA. Pretty disappointing for a product that is brand new and (I can only assume) pretty much came straight to my house from the manufacturer. These must be some of the cheapest batteries ever made if they didn't even have the juice in them to last a few weeks without ever being used. :(
summary: A smaller Imaginext set with a fun theme and plenty of moving parts...

reviewText: This is a pretty basic game.  Roll the dice, move the rockets.  A few of the "strips" have properties that affect your moves. reviewText: My son has the Disney/Pixar Cars Micro Drifters Fast-Flip Carry Case which goes with this and he loves it. This item, however, is not the best race track to get.First, it's a bear to put together. Many different parts and stickers that don't really fit where they are supposed to go, make this at least an hour project for the parent. Maybe more if you aren't good at matching up the diagrams with the instruction sheet, which is not an easy task. I'm not usually one who gets tripped up by instruction sheets, but there are a couple of items that look very similar and are easy to confuse on this one. Also, one of the attachments was so hard to click together right, I spent 15 minutes, just on that one thing.When the track was finally together, we tried it out, but it didn't work exactly right. The cars tend to jam in the pump-action booster and by the third try, I was ready to give up. My son was eager to play, though, so he worked with it for about 20 more turns before the track actually "flipped" like it's supposed to. The track flip was pretty cool, but it doesn't work all the way. The round part of the track flips, but the arm that extends down to the booster only turns half way because it is too big to make a full circle without hitting the ground. For that arm to work, you would have to have two steady surfaces on other end of the track with nothing under that one arm so it could turn full circle. We tried that, but it still had trouble turning all the way around.You get one Lightning McQueen car for this track and the track only works with two cars. Thankfully, my son had another car to use with it. Basically, the first car goes and sets off a lever, then when the second car goes, the track will flip. Without the second car, no flippage.Another problem with this track is that when the cars are "let go" into the booster, they tend to flip over or go sideways, getting stuck in the booster. My son could not figure out how to get them out, so I was fishing them out about every ten minutes. At one point, the booster jammed (after about an hour of play) and we thought it was broke forever. There were no cars inside or jamming the system... after about 30 mins, it miraculously wasn't jammed anymore. After that first jam, it jams every once in awhile... probably about 3 times a day.A safety hazard is needed for anyone sitting next to the track. About every 3rd car will go flying off the track and land across the room. My son loves this, but if he were playing with another kid, he would be black and blue by now.All this said, my son still loves playing with it, because it is cars and because he gets to flip cars across the room, but it does not operate as stated.

reviewText: Five members of my family played this game. Two adults and kids ages: 17, 13, & 11. It is a pretty fast paced game but can be slow due to it taking a few moments for the players to decide who deserves which token at the end of the rounds.The game is for ages 5 and up and for 2 or more players. Although the title is "Don't Make Me Laugh" - the goal is TO LAUGH. It's played in three rounds. Solo Act - the person acts out on their own; Partner Play - choose someone to help you act out your card description; and All Play where everyone does what their card says at the same time. At the end, every player gives out three "awards" (I call them tokens) to the other players. The winner is the one who received the most awards.Contents are: 100 Improv cards, 17 award title cards, 1 clown nose, 5 cloth goodie bags, 55 award tokens, 15 jelly bands (look like bracelets), and a parent guide.So, for some creative silliness with your young kiddos, I recommend this. My 13 year old didn't care for it but my other two really got into character and had fun with it.

reviewText: I got this doll to my 6 year old granddaughter.First, I'll address the packaging.  The packaging is certainly not "frustration free" but it is not as bad some other toys I have gotten.  There are several "straps" that hold the doll to its packaging. Besides the doll, there is a small user-manual or quick start guide.The batteries that come with the doll are "demonstration batteries" which are pre-installed in the doll's shoes.  You'll need a screwdriver to open her shoes and replace the batteries.  Unfortunately, one of the batteries that came with my doll was dead, so I just replaced all of them with fresh AA alkaline batteries.My granddaughter had seen advertising for the doll and she was already familiar with most of its functions.  She knew how to push the belly to get her to talk (Spanish and English).  Walking was a little more tricky for her.  I had to show her how to hold the doll's hands to help her walk, eventually letting the doll walk by herself.  The doll recognizes when she's walking with help or all by herself, and she will speak accordingly.  If she walks by herself and falls, she will ask for help.We tried the doll on ceramic tile, hardwood flooring and low pile carpet.  She was able to "walk" on all of the surfaces.The doll's movement is a bit robotic, and you can hear the servo mechanisms when she walks. Just don't expect a doll that quietly walks smoothly across the floor.The educational value with this doll comes in the form of developing empathy and nurturing skills.  With my granddaughter, I think this doll will easily become one of her favorite toys.

reviewText: I chose this game thinking that it would make a great strategy game for the family to play.  We've owned it for quite some time now, and while I enjoy it, it's definitely not for younger children.  The rules are simple enough for a family to understand; however, the logic that is required to be able to win the game is not something that 9-year old children are generally capable of utilizing.The game itself is interesting.  The players are each architects and the goal is to build towers which earn them prestige points.  The towers are purchased part by part at the marketplace.  The different colors represent the different grades of materials available.  There are enough steps to keep it interesting without becoming overly complex.  As with most logic games, the game is never the exact same twice.  The trick to it is to create the best strategy to get the best pieces and earn more prestige than the other architects.This is definitely a different style of game.  It's all about thinking and strategizing.  I wish that there were a younger version of it.  We have the children's version of Settlers of Catan and Ticket to Ride.  As it stands, it needs to be reserved for older children, teens and adults to avoid frustration.

reviewText: My 4-year old loves Thomas and all things train related.  He was really excited to open this and start using it.  I didn't tell him about the smoke in order to gauge his reaction.  Overall, he liked it, but wasn't overly impressed.  The main disappointment is that the remote control seems flaky, making it very difficult to operate the toy.When the toy works, it's really cool.  The "steam" seems to be cool mist similar to what's produced by an ultrasonic humidifier.  The smoke stack also has a blue LED light that shines whenever it makes the smoke so that you can see it easier.I really liked the fill bottle, which stores on the underside of Thomas, and the train is designed that it leaks very little even if turned upside down.  My son had as much fun refilling Thomas as using him.It worked pretty well on both firm plush and berber carpeting,The remote is IR (infrared) so it has to be close and able to see Thomas.  I noticed that my remote was constantly sending a signal when viewed through a digital camera - not sure if that's a defect or the design.The remote has 3 buttons: Forward, Reverse/turn, and "Special Move".  With our, the buttons simply aren't reliable in that sometimes they work and sometimes they don't.  I've used different sets of batteries, held it at every distance and angle to Thomas, and it's just plain spotty.  At one point my son was so aggravated he was pratically throwing a tantrum - and I couldn't blame him.The forward button makes him go and periodically makes steam.  Reverse does the same.  The middle button causes Thomas to do a variety of special moves on his own like going forward then backward in a complete circle.Just keep in mind that this is a very basic remote controlled toy.  You can't steer Thomas, as he only turns one direction and that is only when going in reverse.  The main draw is the cool steam.  My son played with him for about 2 days straight, but very rarely since then - the novelty wore out quickly.

reviewText: This is a really nerve-wracking--but fun!--game with a real slippery twist on the typical stacking game.Set-Up:The penguins come in three plastic pieces and must be assembled prior to playing. They're a bit tough to snap together, so this is probably best handled by an adult. I got one extra penguin--25 instead of 24. Of course, it's a nice thing to get an extra piece! But I just wanted to mention it since it's a good idea to count the number of penguins you end up with before dividing them up between players, because it may not be 24 as described.Play:Players take turns placing a penguin anywhere on the "ice." The "ice"--or rather, the surface of the plastic--is intentionally extra-slippery, so it's a challenge to get a foothold with the penguins. Typical balance games that I have played don't usually have an extra added feature like this texture--which makes it more of a challenge! Aside from the "ice" being slippery, the iceberg tips in all directions, since it's just sitting atop a center post stand. One nice feature about the game is that you're allowed to spin the iceberg (not the game base) around to look for a decent spot to put a penguin--although that also adds to the risk that penguins will drop. Any penguins that drop on your turn must be taken by you. The goal is to get rid of all of your penguins first.You can think you're winning, and then suddenly--most of the penguins fall and there's no chance! The game is nicely done in that as little as one penguin will fall . . . or a bunch. You just never know.There's also a one-player game--trying to get ALL of the included penguins on the iceberg. It's tricky, because they just barely fit since there's not much room on the little "ice" tiers. But it's possible! (You CAN fit on 25 penguins, if you also get an extra!)This game is really fun, and set-up is simple after the initial penguin assembly. I like the fact that the texture of the ice adds to the challenge, making it not only a weight balancing game, but also one of trying to find a decent foothold for the penguins, so they don't slip off. It's also a neat touch that Ravensburger included a second game option.The only slightly negative thing I can think of is that the penguins are just black and white, with white eyes and a black bow-tie. It would have been nice if orange and red had been added to the color palette. But that's not all that important.
